title: Scarborough calls on Congress to investigate activities at local ICE facility
description:
Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.
ICE in Maine Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center.
The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells.
The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC.
Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly protested outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.
text:
Members of the Scarborough Town Council voted Wednesday to pass a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to look into the operations of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in the town after a federal agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford earlier this month.

But residents who spoke at the town council meeting said the proclamation doesn’t go far enough.

“We’re not in charge of federal immigration policy, but all eyes in Maine are on us as the only town that hosts a facility,” said Mary Ellen Galante, a Scarborough resident and retired nurse midwife, who objected to the proclamation because it “places all of the responsibility for action on our federal delegation and not on our town.”

Galante was among the roughly 70 people who attended the packed meeting, while more than 50 others braved the rain outside holding signs calling to get ICE out of Maine.

New restrictions on state involvement in immigration enforcement take effect Wednesday

The killing of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 has renewed scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement in Maine and many residents have called for local and state leaders to do more to protect communities in the state.

The question of how much power a community has to challenge federal activities within its jurisdiction is one that has wracked the state since President Donald Trump’s administration launched its enhanced enforcement operation in January. Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.

ICE in Maine

Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center. The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells. Detainees have historically been held in local jails or transferred to detention centers in Massachusetts or New Hampshire, or as far as Texas.

But during the meeting, several speakers raised concerns that ICE was misrepresenting what was occurring at that location.

“I think there are legitimate questions about whether the ordinances and the plans that have been put into place are consistent with what is happening in practice there,” Maine Rep. Sophie Warren, a Democrat who represents Scarborough, told Maine Morning Star. Warren presented a petition signed by more than 370 Mainers, 175 of which are Scarborough residents, calling on the council to take specific actions, including formally investigating the operations at the ICE facility and enforcing local laws and other municipal tools to rein in unlawful activities, which she said has precedence in Oregon.

The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC. According to the agency’s lease inventory, the current 15-year lease began in 2021.

Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly protested outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts made an unannounced visit to the facility on July 17, during which he said he confirmed that is where the officer who shot Guerrero works.

In December, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree also visited the building on Manson Libby Rd. after concerns were raised about attorneys not being permitted to accompany their clients to routine check-ins.

Josh Soley, the leasing and property manager for the building, said the GSA has the authority to subleaseto whichever agency they choose and that neither the state nor landlord has a say in who occupies the building.

Soley said he’s in support of the protests but believes the facility has nothing to do with what happened in Biddeford. He said people are “trying to find a place to put their voice, but I think it needs to be better targeted.”

But Scarborough councilmember Jon Anderson said that he believes Soley “must be part of this conversation.” Anderson said residents should know whether the company intends to extend the lease when it expires, and said Soley should also explore whether there’s a “mutually agreeable path” to end the lease arrangement with GSA early, “given the tragedy that occurred from the ICE agent employed at that facility.”

GSA declined to comment on the proclamation or the terms of the current lease agreement.

“I have a 20-page lease that I need to re-sign every single year and it asks me not to do unlawful activity,” Scarborough resident Sarah Lunt told the council. She added, “I would assume that that includes murdering someone in cold blood.”

Proclamation details

The proclamation asks Maine’s congressional delegation to engage with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and other agencies to review the facility and evaluate alternatives, “including the relocation or discontinuation of such operations at that location.”

It further asks for transparency and community engagement regarding federal immigration enforcement activities and for the delegation to “ensure that federal actions conducted within Maine respect human dignity, civil rights, public trust, due process, and community safety and commit to raising concerns with federal officials should evidence emerge that these standards are not being upheld.”

The town notes the proclamation should not be interpreted as opposition to lawful immigration enforcement but rather, the “expectation that such enforcement be conducted in a manner consistent with the values of safety, transparency, accountability, and respect for all people.”

While a handful of residents expressed concern that the resolution was beyond the purview of the council and would open the town to lawsuits from the federal government, the vast majority who spoke said they supported the proclamation as a first step for the town to take.

Congressional support

Ahead of the meeting, Pingree, who represents the southern Maine district that includes Biddeford and Scarborough, told the Scarborough council that the town “has every right to ask whether continuing to host this facility serves the interests of the community.”

“In my view, that question deserves serious consideration from the Department of Homeland Security,” Pingree wrote in a letter. “When a federal facility reaches the point where its very presence undermines the public confidence and leaves residents feeling less safe, the federal government has a responsibility to reconsider if that facility belongs there at all.”

Pingree added that she’s “exploring every available avenue to address enforcement operations and the continued presence of ICE in Scarborough.”

U.S. Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, and U.S. Rep. Jared Golden did not comment on the proclamation. They previously sent a joint letter to the DHS Inspector General calling for a full, transparent investigation into the shooting and King has called for a review of ICE protocol.

title: Ohio Haitians lose jobs, face terror — and impossible choices
authors: Marty Schladen, Siddarth Sivaraman, Megan Henry
description:
With Ohio’s Haitian refugees losing their protected status Monday, Springfield’s large population has begun being terminated from their jobs, a pastor who works with the community said on Tuesday.
Early last year, Ohio’s then-Attorney General Dave Yost and 27 other Republican state AGs wrote a letter to the Trump administration stressing the word “temporary” in temporary protected status.
They claimed without evidence that it was safe for some with protected status to return to those home countries and urged a review.
Lawyers for the Haitians sued, arguing that Noem had failed to follow the 1990 law creating temporary protected status.
But for Haitians in Ohio, that might seem a thin reed on which to lean.
text:
With Ohio’s Haitian refugees losing their protected status Monday, Springfield’s large population has begun being terminated from their jobs, a pastor who works with the community said on Tuesday.

Without legal status, their work permits become invalid. They also face being forced to return to a nation that the International Rescue Committee says is “in the grip of an overwhelming humanitarian crisis.”

Right now, gangs control Haiti. Kidnapping, murder, and rape are rampant. And the pastor, Carl Ruby, said one Springfield 12-year-old faces having to return to a place where he saw animals feeding on murdered corpses when he was just five.

‘Thousands of people are now going to die violent deaths,’ says attorney for Ohio Haitian community

“They’re just terrified for their physical safety,” Ruby said during a virtual press conference. “Many of them have already been traumatized… Some of them have been in prison. Some of them have been tortured. Some have been beaten. Some had been raped. Nearly all of them have seen friends or family members killed.”

And some of those families — those who have had children since coming to the United States — face an excruciating choice: whether to take their children with them into the violent chaos that is Haiti or leave them behind in a relatively peaceful, prosperous place where their children’s citizenship gives them the right to stay.

More than 330,000 Haitians have received temporary-protected status since an earthquake devastated the impoverished Caribbean country in 2010. Once in the United States, their status has been renewed as conditions in Haiti continued to deteriorate.

Early last year, Ohio’s then-Attorney General Dave Yost and 27 other Republican state AGs wrote a letter to the Trump administration stressing the word “temporary” in temporary protected status.

They claimed without evidence that it was safe for some with protected status to return to those home countries and urged a review.

Then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in November announced that she was terminating protected status for Haitians who had qualified, including about 45,000 in Ohio and roughly 15,000 in Springfield.

Lawyers for the Haitians sued, arguing that Noem had failed to follow the 1990 law creating temporary protected status. It requires that the government conduct a mandatory review of conditions in a group’s home country to certify that it’s safe to return before forcing them to go.

Lower courts blocked the termination.

But in June, in a 6-3 ruling the U.S. Supreme Court reversed them, ruling that the TPS law itself barred most court challenges to the way its provisions were or were not applied.

Attempt to halt imminent deportations of Haitians and Syrians blocked in US Senate

The court didn’t bar constitutional challenges, however, and SCOTUS Blog on Tuesday reported that some of those are in the works.

But for Haitians in Ohio, that might seem a thin reed on which to lean. They and many others are bracing for a mass-deportation such as those conducted by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in other regions.

Ruby, the Springfield pastor, said no such operation has happened yet.

“It could happen as soon as this week,” he said. “What we’re hearing from other reporting is that they’re planning on deporting them directly back to Haiti. There have been cases in the community where they have been picked up one day. Sent to a detention center the next day. And on the third or the fourth day they’re back in Haiti. It’s obviously not safe for them to go there.”

The pastor added that jobs and support services are almost nonexistent when deportees get to Haiti.

In addition to terror over what might happen in Haiti are worries about what’s next for Springfield.

Ruby said that he and his colleagues have been working for the past 18 months to build “a very large coalition of faith leaders not only here in Springfield, but across the state of Ohio and across the nation who will stand with us if we have anything like what took place in Minneapolis.”

He was referring to a mass-enforcement operation last winter in which masked ICE officers shot and killed two protestors, both of them citizens. Analysis of videos taken at the scene showed that neither protester posed the threat that Trump administration officials claimed after the shootings.

Ruby stressed that he and other faith leaders want any protests of ICE enforcement actions to be peaceful, and that protesters have to be ready for the possible consequences of civil disobedience, such as going to jail.

Gov. Mike DeWine has criticized some of his Republican colleagues for falsely demonizing Springfield’s Haitian immigrants.

On Tuesday, his spokesman reiterated a statement DeWine issued last month when the U.S. Supreme Court issued its ruling that effectively revoked their protected status.

“Today’s decision is a legal decision,” DeWine said. “As I have stated in the past, the policy to remove these individuals from this country is a mistake.”

DeWine later added, “The situation in Haiti could hardly be much worse. The violent gangs run most of the country. The government barely functions. And, the economy is in shambles.”

Lynn Tramonte, founder of the Ohio Immigrant Alliance, questioned whether DeWine would instruct the Ohio Highway Patrol not to assist ICE in enforcement operations.

In the past, the Highway Patrol has worked with U.S. Border Patrol to apprehend undocumented immigrants, the American Immigration Council reports.

Dan Tierney, DeWine’s press secretary, didn’t answer directly when asked if the Highway Patrol would assist ICE with enforcement operations in Springfield.

Tramonte said DeWine could do more to help Haitians who suddenly find themselves without status.

“The governor might claim he is powerless to do anything in the face of federal agents invading our state to take our people, but here are two things he can do,” Tramonte said in a text message.

“He can instruct the Highway Patrol not to assist ICE in the enforcement of civil immigration laws. That’s not their job and they shouldn’t have to get involved. He can also underscore the same point for local police who often seem to think they should be on the hunt for immigrants instead of focusing on crime.”

text:
Emily Scolnick is a 2026 Dow Jones News Fund intern at the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.

Immigration advocates from across Pennsylvania called on Gov. Josh Shapiro to shut down a youth detention center in Berks County and end state collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Wednesday.

Over 100 people from 15 Pennsylvania counties joined a rally on the Capitol steps, urging Shapiro to protect immigrant communities, limit the enforcement of ICE detainers, and prevent ICE from accessing state databases and information from PennDOT that could lead to enforcement efforts.

“Imagine waking up every day and knowing that going to work could separate you from your family,” said Vincent Nguyen, a youth leader with the Woori Center and intern with the Pennsylvania Immigration Coalition (PIC), at a press conference Wednesday. “My generation is inheriting Pennsylvania, the United States, that today’s leaders are shaping. I want to inherit a commonwealth where every family can … live without fear.”

The Shapiro administration said it is currently reviewing how ICE, Customs and Border Protection, and other federal agencies can access state systems. Pennsylvania State Police officers are also not permitted to detain individuals due to their immigration status.

Several attendees said Shapiro’s response moving forward — or lack thereof — could determine how they vote in November’s election, where he is running for a second term against Republican and current state Treasurer Stacy Garrity.

“You want our vote, you earn our vote,” Jasmine Rivera, PIC’s executive director, said at the rally. “You are not getting a dime of our money until you finally do something.”

Nguyen told the Capital-Star that he and many other young people “aren’t just voting for the party anymore. They’re voting for the person.”

“I think it’s time that Josh Shapiro and many other politicians realize that they won’t get our support just because we may sort of agree with them on some things,” he said.

Tammy Murphy, the public policy and advocacy manager for Make the Road PA, said politicians can’t hide from the immigration issue going into this year’s elections. She added that while she won’t vote for Garrity, that doesn’t mean Shapiro will get her vote if he does not act.

“I’m an immigrant myself, formerly undocumented,” said Miguel Andrade, who is the communications director for PIC, but shared his personal views. “It’s a personal issue for me, and it does make me think about who are the elected officials I’m going to be supporting moving forward.”

“I would not vote for Shapiro in this moment,” he added.

Calls to close Abraxas

Many rally attendees displayed signs calling for Shapiro to issue an Emergency Removal Order to close Abraxas Academy, a youth detention center in Berks County that has faced several lawsuits alleging sexual abuse within the facility this year.

“A society is measured by how we treat our most vulnerable members, especially those who are in prison and children,” said David Wesley Cornish, an attorney representing multiple Abraxas victims. “Children are to be protected and cared for. They are to be nurtured. They are not to be harmed.”

Rosie Lapowsky, a spokesperson for Shapiro, wrote in a statement that Pennsylvania’s Department of Human Services currently performs weekly unannounced visits to Abraxas to inspect living conditions and assess treatment of its youth.

“The Shapiro Administration has zero tolerance for any neglect, abuse or mistreatment of children in facilities it licenses,” she wrote. “Our priority is keeping these children safe — and we are mindful that if an Emergency Removal Order were to be issued for Abraxas Academy, non-citizen youth would be transferred back into the custody of the Trump Administration, at which point Pennsylvania would no longer have the oversight authority to ensure they are being cared for.”

In November 2025, DHS revoked Abraxas’ license for its Secure Detention Unit — one of three licenses the facility maintains — for failure to report alleged instances of abuse. Lapowsky said there has been no new evidence that has prompted additional investigation.

The other two licenses continue to be subject to increased monitoring from DHS, which has no role in placing non-citizen children, according to the Shapiro administration.

“Every leader, every lawmaker, every citizen of Pennsylvania should be demanding the immediate release of these youth and the immediate closure of the Abraxas facility,” said Leslie Mamas, a reverend at the United Church of Christ in Montgomery County. “This isn’t a political issue. It is a moral one.”

Following the rally, Rivera led a group of organizers to Shapiro’s office to deliver a letter signed by immigrant rights advocates. The contents have not been released publicly.

She said up to this point, there have been no direct conversations with the governor about the coalition’s demands, “and it’s not for lack of asking.”

“There’s been many, many, many conversations and research and reports sent over to his staff,” she added.

title: Can the UN's Refugee Convention survive? - Al Jazeera
description:
The humanitarian disaster prompted the United Nations to agree on a comprehensive legal framework outlining states’ obligations to protect refugees.
This became the 1951 Refugee Convention, which initially applied to Europeans but was subsequently amended in 1967 to apply to all those fleeing persecution.
Today, 149 nations are parties to the convention and no country has ever withdrawn from it.

text:
At the end of World War II, great swaths of Europe lay in ruins and millions had been forcibly displaced.

The humanitarian disaster prompted the United Nations to agree on a comprehensive legal framework outlining states’ obligations to protect refugees. This became the 1951 Refugee Convention, which initially applied to Europeans but was subsequently amended in 1967 to apply to all those fleeing persecution. Today, 149 nations are parties to the convention and no country has ever withdrawn from it.

At least, not yet.

Nearly eight decades later, the world is struggling. The Syrian civil war triggered an enormous influx of refugees into Europe. Now, millions of refugees have fled Sudan’s brutal civil war, state collapse in Venezuela has caused mass migration, and the Russian invasion of Ukraine and many other conflicts around the world are in full swing, again causing mass displacements.

The UN currently records more than 41 million refugees worldwide.

The UN convention defines a refugee as a person who is outside their country of origin with a “well-founded fear of being persecuted for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion”. The principle of non-refoulement – the stipulation that a refugee should not be returned to a country where they could be harmed – is a cornerstone of the treaty.

In recent years, some of the world’s richest countries have begun to roll out increasingly punitive policies towards refugees as populist, anti-immigration sentiment has taken hold.

Last month the Supreme Court ruled in favour of allowing the Trump administration to turn back asylum seekers at the border and remove temporary protected status (TPS) from Haitians and Syrians. This year refugee admissions to the US have been almost exclusively white South Africans.

Refugees attempting to reach Australia by boat are now either turned back at sea or sent to offshore detention facilities, leading to strong criticism from human rights organisations on the Pacific island of Nauru.

Denmark, which was the first country to sign the convention three-quarters of a century ago, has stripped Syrian refugees of legal status and threatened them with deportation after deeming those from Damascus and surrounding regions safe, despite the country still being under the control of the Assad regime at the time. It passed a sweeping package of reforms in 2019.

A decade on from the refugee crisis, fuelled by the Syrian war and which saw more than one million people flee to Europe, border guards in several European Union states now routinely conduct violent pushbacks. Greece turns back boats while Poland forces them over the border into Belarus.

‘Share, not shift, responsibilities’

For campaigners, new European policies fly in the face of the convention’s principles, such as the right to territorial asylum and the principle of non-refoulement.

Adriana Tidona, migration researcher at Amnesty International, told Al Jazeera: “The new Migration and Asylum Pact will make it easier for EU countries to reject asylum applications without review, and send people to so-called ‘safe third countries’ to which they have no connection and where they have never even set foot.”

The 75th anniversary of the convention, Tidona said, is “an urgent reminder of the need to re-centre international cooperation in refugee protection and to share, not shift, responsibilities.

In the United States, the Trump administration is reportedly mulling withdrawing support from the UN refugee agency UNHCR, amid accusations that it pursues “a mass migration agenda”. It has also recently removed “protected status” for Syrian and Haitian nationals.

But for proponents of refugee rights, the Refugee Convention has its own limitations anyway.

While tens of millions have benefitted from its protection from persecution since 1951, others who are escaping different kinds of hardship such as poverty, climate change, natural disasters or gang violence, do not necessarily qualify under the criteria.

Without any specific court or treaty which can oversee and punish breaches, governments tend to interpret the convention according to their interests or even flout it altogether, experts say. According to Jeff Crisp at the Oxford University Refugee Studies Centre, who is also former head of policy development and evaluation at UNHCR, this is by design.

“The convention wouldn’t have been set up if there was enforcement,” he told Al Jazeera. “And the lack of it has become evident as the atmosphere around refugee protection has become more toxic.”

In recent years, Western governments have gone further than enacting anti-refugee policies; they have actively deported people to third countries to which they have no connection.

The former Conservative government in the United Kingdom sought to send asylum seekers to Rwanda, until the policy was overturned by the new Labour government in 2024. Italy has set up detention facilities in Albania and the US has sent deportees from multiple nationalities to countries including Iran, South Sudan and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

Several EU countries, including Germany, Austria and the Netherlands, are now exploring the establishment of “return hubs” in Asian and African countries to process asylum seekers who cannot be returned to their home countries.

As states increasingly reinterpret or even flout the convention’s principles, Susan Fratzke, senior policy analyst at the Migration Policy Institute, said an update could address some of the existing gaps.

“A new protocol would avoid reopening some of the fundamental parts of the convention like the definition of a refugee and the principle of non-refoulement,” she told Al Jazeera.

“But by providing states with a sound legal basis for implementing more restrictive policies like safe third country or returns policies, you could also open up more protections for refugees like integration and the right to work.”

Removing safe routes

While the convention states that they should not be punished for entering countries irregularly to claim asylum, European governments from Greece to the UK have been detaining refugees under anti-smuggling laws in recent years.

At the same time, many of the same countries have removed or restricted safe routes for refugees such as family reunion pathways or resettlement schemes.

In 2025, only 37,000 refugees were resettled by UNHCR, down from 116,000 in 2024. With legal avenues disappearing and while people are required to be physically present in a country to access its asylum system, they are therefore increasingly reliant on smugglers to facilitate their movement.

About 65 percent of the world’s refugees have fled to neighbouring countries, meaning that the responsibility of hosting displaced populations primarily falls on the shoulders of low or middle-income countries.

Findings this month by polling company Ipsos, which questioned 21,000 people in 29 countries, suggest that public attitudes towards refugees may not be as hostile as politicians and media often claim, though it is still a mixed picture.

While two-thirds of Ipsos respondents said they support giving refuge to those fleeing war and persecution, a similar proportion questioned whether those claiming to be in need are indeed genuine. On whether borders should be closed to refugees, 49 percent agreed while 41 percent disagreed.

Ultimately, according to Crisp from Oxford University, there is no “big bang solution” for reform.

“We may have to accept the fact that the convention or a variant of it will remain, though not respected in practice, and governments will continue to take unilateral actions.”

And, Crisp warns, while Western countries may wish to reduce refugee protections, there may not be international consensus.

“So far the whole debate has been on the Global North’s terms, but the Global South may be resistant to making major changes, especially externalisation and containment policies that lead to a greater proportion of refugees remaining in their region.”

text:
As temporary protected status expires for many Haitian and Syrian immigrants following a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision, Worcester’s Human Rights Commission is preparing for what local officials say could be significant impacts on residents, employers and immigrant families across the city.

During Monday night’s meeting, Human Rights Specialist Justo Soto of the city’s Executive Office of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion gave an overview of the federal changes and the resources available to affected residents, stressing that the briefing was for informational purposes and not as legal advice.

“The purpose of this presentation is to provide key information about the recent U.S. Supreme Court decision affecting temporary protected status … and the upcoming deadline for those on TPS,” Soto said.

Temporary protected status, commonly known as TPS, allows eligible nationals of designated countries to remain legally in the United States when conditions such as armed conflict, natural disasters or other extraordinary circumstances make returning home unsafe.

The designation also allows recipients to obtain work authorization and, in some cases, travel authorization. It does not, however, provide a direct path to permanent residency or U.S. citizenship.

Soto told commissioners that Haiti and Syria are among the countries most immediately affected by the Supreme Court’s decision, which allows the federal government to move forward with terminating Haiti’s TPS designation while additional legal challenges continue.

He said the decision does not determine whether Haiti is safe to return to and does not automatically make every TPS holder subject to deportation. Individual immigration cases, he said, continue to be evaluated under existing immigration law.

Soto also highlighted efforts already underway in Worcester to help affected residents.

He said Mayor Joe Petty and U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern met earlier this month to discuss the impact of TPS changes on Worcester residents. A second meeting focused on connecting residents with legal resources, employer guidance and community organizations that can help immigrants understand their options.

Soto said city officials are encouraging employers not to immediately terminate workers whose TPS-based employment authorization is expiring and instead explore whether employees may qualify for other forms of work authorization or immigration relief.

He also discussed growing concerns over immigration court proceedings.

According to Soto, immigration courts have been scheduling large “mega master calendar” hearings involving dozens of cases at once. He said immigrant advocacy organizations have reported that some individuals have failed to appear after hearing dates were moved, resulting in removal orders being issued in their absence.

The Immigrant Justice Network of Massachusetts has reported those proceedings are occurring regularly in Worcester, Soto said.

Human Rights Commission Chairman Randy Feldman said another recent change requires most immigrants to appear in person for immigration proceedings rather than by video, increasing the importance of receiving accurate hearing notices.

Feldman also said work authorization for many Haitian and Syrian TPS recipients expired this week, creating uncertainty for affected workers and employers.

At the same time, he noted that many Haitian residents have already filed asylum applications, meaning the expiration of TPS does not necessarily end their ability to remain in the United States while those cases proceed.

Toward the end of the meeting, Feldman said the commission hopes to invite representatives from Legal Services of Central Massachusetts to a future meeting to explain the legal assistance available to immigrants facing changing federal policies.

name: Human Rights
title: In Its Second Term, Trump Administration Quietly Expands Family Separation
description:
Unlike in the first Trump term, recent separations are a largely indirect consequence of heightened enforcement, rather than an intentional policy choice.
There is evidence that the number of children separated from their parents has far surpassed that of the first Trump term.
After the Biden administration’s closure in 2021 of all federal family detention facilities, located in Texas and Pennsylvania, the Trump administration in 2025 reopened family detention space in Texas.
This idea was dismissed by the Obama administration but was later implemented during the first Trump term.
All the same, the Trump administration has invested significant resources into locating these children and establishing other child-safety oversight initiatives.
text:
With minimal public scrutiny, U.S. authorities have separated an unknown but likely significant number of children from their parents as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportations effort during its second term. While perhaps occurring with greater frequency, these separations are happening in more diffuse ways and locations than the dramatic, border-related incidents of the first term, which resulted in troubling images of young children huddled behind chain-link fencing in warehouse-like shelters.

Unlike in the first Trump term, recent separations are a largely indirect consequence of heightened enforcement, rather than an intentional policy choice. They are the result of the assertive enforcement push and looser restrictions on arresting parents, as many unauthorized immigrants have been swiftly deported, leaving their children behind, or, facing the threat of deportation, have conceded to voluntarily depart the United States. The separations also stem from different practices than in the first term, often occurring after parents are detained in traffic stops, at workplaces, and elsewhere in U.S. communities, rather than at the U.S.-Mexico border.

For these and other reasons, the public response has been more muted. Whereas public backlash and global attention led to the quick termination of the “zero-tolerance” policy that drove thousands of parent-child separations during the first Trump term, the current approach has unfolded quietly for well more than a year.

Because of the decentralized nature of these separations and the general opacity about the arrests, detention, and removals occurring during the second Trump term, it is unclear precisely how many parents have been deported without their children or how often the threat of separation has been used to induce “self-deportation,” with or without the children.

For many families, however—including many U.S.-citizen children—the consequences are the same as before. Frequently, separated children have been left in the care of extended family or handed over to the federal Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), where they are classified as unaccompanied minors. Research has shown that the trauma of separation can have lifelong repercussions, including on mental and physical health and development.

At the same time, the administration has seemed to deprioritize reconnecting the children who were separated from their parents during its first term, which was a focus of the Biden administration. It has also slashed federal funding for children’s legal representation in immigration court and connected child-welfare efforts with its immigration enforcement mission, not least by involving agents in welfare checks and sharing sensitive ORR data with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), leading to more than 12,000 arrests according to internal government data reviewed by Reuters.

This article provides an overview of family separations and the welfare policies governing the wellbeing of migrant children during President Donald Trump’s second term. It traces the rise in detention and removal of noncitizen parents and compares it with the era of separations linked to the first term’s zero-tolerance policy. It also tracks the changing focus for reunification and child-protection mechanisms and the emergence of child-linked enforcement initiatives.

How the Mass Deportation Push Separates Families

After the major controversy over family separation during the first Trump term, during which several thousand children were separated from a parent, the Biden administration declared that unauthorized immigrants in immigration proceedings who are parents be detained only in “limited circumstances.” A July 2025 ICE directive rescinded those limitations, gave broad discretion to detain and remove parents, and abolished a requirement to place detained parents as “close as practicable” to their minor children.

This loosening of guidelines, combined with scaled-up immigration enforcement, has resulted in the detention of thousands of parents, many of whose minor children are U.S. citizens. Of the 320,000 book-ins to detention that ICE has reported so far in fiscal year (FY) 2026, nearly 17,900 (6 percent) were of people who self-reported they were parents of U.S.-citizen children—an almost twofold increase over FY 2024 (see Figure 1). This is likely a dramatic undercount given that many parents may decline to identify themselves as such, potentially out of fear of further involvement with immigration enforcement. This number also does not include the parents of noncitizen children, who may or may not also be targeted for enforcement, nor would it include the detention in state and local jails of noncitizens identified for removal by state and local law enforcement working with ICE but not yet in ICE’s database. As such, it is unclear how many children in total have had a parent detained by immigration enforcement officials during this administration.

There is evidence that the number of children separated from their parents has far surpassed that of the first Trump term. The Brookings Institution has estimated that approximately 205,000 children, 71 percent of them U.S. citizens, had a parent detained by immigration officials as of May 2026. In total, the Migration Policy Institute (MPI) estimates that 6.3 million children in the United States were living with at least one parent who was an unauthorized immigrant as of mid-2023, 84 percent of whom were U.S. citizens.

ICE also appears to be using the threat of separation as leverage to convince unauthorized immigrant parents to voluntarily leave the United States with their children. Journalists, lawyers, and others have documented cases of detained parents given the option to leave voluntarily with their children or contest their removal in immigration court and see their children sent to a federal shelter. To avoid separation, some parents have left the United States even if they have an asylum claim or another basis to remain in the United States, in a practice critics describe as coercive.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has denied that this approach amounts to a family separation policy, stating that parents have the choice to either depart the country as a family or refuse and face immigration enforcement consequences.

After the Biden administration’s closure in 2021 of all federal family detention facilities, located in Texas and Pennsylvania, the Trump administration in 2025 reopened family detention space in Texas. It has sought to expand detention capacity to hold families and unaccompanied children, including with a proposed facility in Alexandria, Louisiana that is being set up as a holding center for families that have agreed to departure. The planned 528-bed facility is near an airport hub that has been used to facilitate thousands of deportation flights.

Amid rising family arrivals, the then executive associate director of ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations, Tom Homan, in 2014 reportedly proposed detaining parents, which would inevitably result in family separation and as a result act as a deterrent. This idea was dismissed by the Obama administration but was later implemented during the first Trump term. In 2018, the Justice Department announced a zero-tolerance policy at the U.S.-Mexico border, mandating criminal prosecution of everyone entering or re-entering the United States without authorization—primarily between ports of entry—including parents travelling with children.

Because children cannot be criminally charged as adults for the standard immigration crimes of illegal entry or illegal re-entry or be detained in adult facilities, they were separated from their accompanying parent. DHS treated these children as having no parent or legal guardian in the United States able to provide care, and therefore legally designated them as unaccompanied. In accordance with the 2008 Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, the children were transferred within 72 hours to ORR, an office of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), until they could be released to a sponsoring parent or other qualified adult who could provide for their wellbeing.

ORR shelters were often overcrowded, featured chain-link fences, and resembled prison-like conditions that shocked the public. Scenes sometimes described as “kids in cages” became emblematic of what critics decried as the Trump administration’s harsh enforcement policies and resulted in widespread public opposition, in particular after audio of sobbing children in one facility was leaked. The administration terminated the policy in June 2018, only two months after it had been implemented. Days later, a federal judge ordered a halt to the zero-tolerance policy and demanded the reunification of separated families.

Still, for various reasons, many additional children were separated from their parents after the court order. The chaotic nature of the process meant that there are no complete, official data, and the true number of separations remains unclear. The Biden administration said in 2024 that it had identified 4,656 children who had been separated, although other estimates have stretched above 5,300. Roughly 39 percent of the 2,654 children recorded as separated by mid-2018 were under age 10.

Failure to Reunite All Families

With hasty separations, officials struggled to identify, track, and reunite families after the zero-tolerance policy ended. Hundreds of parents had been deported by the time the government sought to reunite them, further complicating the effort. The Trump administration said in September 2018 that it had reunited or otherwise released 2,167 children over age 5, but public information about its reunification efforts is limited and how many children the administration actually reconnected with their families remains unconfirmed.

Upon taking office, the Biden administration created a task force to identify and reunite families, contributing to the reunification of 3,225 children as of March 2024, the most recent date for which data are available. The Biden administration also issued a directive to avoid family separation except in the “most extreme” circumstances. The Trump administration rescinded that order on its first day in office. It is unclear whether it has continued reunification efforts, and, if so, how effective it has been.

The Trump administration has also sought to weaken family reunification mechanisms, including by terminating the Legal Access Services for Reunified Families (LASRF) Program, which provided free legal access and orientation services to separated families, following the 2018 lawsuit against the zero-tolerance policy. In its final ten months, the program served 1,200 participants. A federal court ordered the Justice Department to reinstate LASRF, but it is unclear the extent to which it had complied as of this writing.

Changes Blur the Line Between Child Protection and Enforcement

Instead of reuniting families separated during its first term, the Trump administration has focused on locating children it alleges had been lost by the Biden administration as well as creating processes for increasing oversight of children’s welfare. At times, these efforts have dovetailed with its broader enforcement agenda.

In responding to large numbers of unaccompanied minors arriving at the border, the Biden administration moved to quickly release children from ORR custody to free up limited bed space and avoid long stays. To do so, it relied on looser vetting of sponsors, who typically are a parent or other relative, leading some children to be placed in questionable or unverified situations. For instance, 16 percent of cases from early 2021 lacked any documentation that one or more required sponsor safety checks had been completed.

A 2024 DHS inspector general report found that ICE did not serve notices to appear in immigration court to 291,000 children between 2019 and 2024; 32,000 unaccompanied minors also did not show up for their immigration court dates between 2019 and 2023. Trump has described these children as missing. “When you talk about separation, we have 325,000 children here during Democrats—and this was done by Democrats—who are right now slaves, sex slaves or dead,” he said in a 2024 TIME magazine interview, although there is no evidence for such outcomes and much of the period cited occurred during his first term.

Although ICE has acknowledged that not issuing notices to appear limits its contact with migrant children, thereby reducing opportunities to verify their safety, it has not claimed that these children are unaccounted for or in danger.

All the same, the Trump administration has invested significant resources into locating these children and establishing other child-safety oversight initiatives. It launched two separate efforts, the Unaccompanied Alien Children (UAC) Joint Initiative and the UAC Safety Verification Initiative, designed to ensure unaccompanied minors meet their reporting obligations and allow investigators to verify they are not being exploited, abused, or trafficked. The investigations include unannounced home visits by DHS and Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) officials, which the Trump administration describes as “welfare checks” but which critics say serve as a pretext to carry out arrests and instill fear. In a two-month period this year, at least 100 children were transferred to ORR custody after their family members were detained or deported following a welfare check.

Similarly, ORR in 2025 tightened requirements for potential sponsors, including mandating fingerprint-based background checks for every adult in the home and demanding DNA tests. While described as efforts to ensure children’s safety, advocates claim that the additional measures intimidate would-be sponsors and discourage some from reuniting with children. Amid these changes, the length of time that children have spent in ORR custody sharply increased, from an average of 30 days in FY 2024 to 117 days in FY 2025 (see Figure 3).

name: Human Rights
title: Immigrant detention should not be a death sentence - The Hill
authors: Raul Reyes, opinion contributor, Raul Reyes, opinion contributor
description:
Paktiawal’s death is part of a grim pattern of increasing deaths in ICE detention.
The U.S. runs the world’s largest immigration detention system, with more than 65,000 people in custody.
Based on these statistics, it’s likely that ICE detention practices violate the law.
The rise in detention deaths includes an “alarming” spike in suicides, according to an Associated Press investigation.
Besides, many conservatives describe themselves as pro-life and say that “All Lives Matter.” How are these principles compatible with the status quo in immigration detention?
text:
Mohammad Nazeer Paktiawal, 41, was dropping two of his children off at preschool in Richardson, Texas, when he was surrounded by masked immigration agents and taken away. Less than 24 hours later, he was dead. Government officials said that Paktiawal, an Afghan national, died due to an “adverse drug reaction.” His March 14 death was ruled to be an accident, although his death certificate was only released this month.

Paktiawal’s death is part of a grim pattern of increasing deaths in ICE detention. The available data suggest that ICE is disregarding its responsibilities to care for detainees. More troubling is the fact that ICE has taken steps to reduce transparency, while the head of Homeland Security has downplayed the extent of this crisis.

The U.S. runs the world’s largest immigration detention system, with more than 65,000 people in custody. However, as the number of detainees has grown, so have the number of fatalities. More than 50 detainees have died during President Trump’s second term, at an average rate of one death every six days. The current mortality rate of those in detention is nearly four times that of the Biden administration.

Based on these statistics, it’s likely that ICE detention practices violate the law. Under the due process clause of the Fifth and 14th Amendments, immigrant detainees are supposed to be protected against harmful conditions. The Supreme Court has ruled that the government must meet the “basic human needs” of the people it confines, while the Immigration and Nationality Act requires that federal officials provide “acceptable conditions” for detention. Moreover, the U.S. is a signatory to international human rights agreements that apply to all people, regardless of immigration status.

It’s hard to square these legal obligations with the reality of our detention system, which has long been plagued by reports of inhumane conditions and inadequate medical care. The rise in detention deaths includes an “alarming” spike in suicides, according to an Associated Press investigation.

The administration’s response to the rising number of detainee deaths is to change the way it reports them. Previously, ICE had to review all detainee deaths, including those that happened up to 30 days after a person’s release. Now the agency is only counting deaths that occur in custody, meaning that ICE can release detainees whose deaths are imminent with no responsibility. ICE has also announced that it will be releasing less information about deaths in detention, with fewer details. So instead of implementing reforms that could save lives, ICE is taking steps to insulate itself from accountability.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has shown indifference to deaths in detention. At a June congressional hearing, he sparred with Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.), asserting that inmates in Illinois state prisons were more likely to die than migrants in ICE detention. He pointed out that ICE has one doctor per thousand detainees — as if that were enough — compared to a lower ratio in Illinois’s correctional facilities. Yet inmates in Illinois correctional facilities have been charged, tried and convicted of crimes. The same cannot be said for people in detention, 70 percent of whom have no criminal record.

Asked by Underwood if DHS had any policies or goals to reduce deaths in custody, Mullin responded, “We’re doing a wonderful job.” Meanwhile, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has called for an investigation into deaths in detention, and Mexico plans to seek criminal charges in the U.S. in response to the deaths of Mexican nationals in detention and during ICE operations.

True, President Trump was elected because he promised to crack down on illegal immigration. But ICE’s own website states that detention is not punitive; it is a place to hold people before their immigration hearings or removal proceedings. As the highest-funded U.S. law enforcement agency, with a $85 billion budget, ICE has no excuse for not providing better for individuals in its care.

For those who may feel that detainees deserve to suffer for entering the country illegally, consider Paktiawal. In his home country, he fought alongside U.S. Special Forces, before being evacuated to the U.S. during the withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021. He had no criminal history. What he did have was a pending asylum claim, meaning he was on a lawful path to remain here. Besides, many conservatives describe themselves as pro-life and say that “All Lives Matter.” How are these principles compatible with the status quo in immigration detention?

Deaths in detention deserve the same scrutiny as high-profile, public killings by immigration agents. Lawmakers need to continue to demand transparency from ICE about its standards, and claw back funding if necessary. Political candidates would do well to spotlight the detention crisis as much as possible.

Being placed in detention should not be a death sentence. Our immigration facilities must respect the rule of law, accountability and human lives.

title: ICE agent in Biddeford shooting was involved in a nearly identical traffic stop
description:
More than a month before an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, the same agent was involved in a similar vehicle stop.
ICE agents pulled up beside his car and told him to get out.
Chatterjee said he had never seen ICE agents smash car windows before Trump returned to office.

She’s leading an effort to help cities and states hold ICE agents accountable in those incidents.
text:
More than a month before an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot and killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, the same agent was involved in a similar vehicle stop.

In both cases, David Brouillette and other ICE officers surveilled a house, looking for the owner of a car at that address. The car pulled out. The man driving was from Latin America, but was neither the owner of the car nor the target of the operation.

The agents made their move anyway.

In the earlier arrest, which happened in Androscoggin County, the man was taken into custody without violence. Immigration attorney Shaan Chatterjee’s firm represented the man and said Brouillette was not the one who handcuffed him.

“Brouillette had an ancillary role in the apprehension of my client,” Chatterjee said. “My client and I are grateful for that, in retrospect.” The man has been released on bond.

In Guerrero’s case, it’s still not clear what happened leading up to the shooting on July 13. The Department of Homeland Security has not confirmed Brouillette was the shooter, though his ex-wife identified him. No video has surfaced to show the interaction; the agents were reportedly wearing body cameras that couldn’t be turned on; and ICE has only said that its agents attempted to conduct a vehicle stop and the car attempted to flee, without providing evidence.

It’s one of many instances in Maine this year where ICE agents have stopped people in cars, sometimes without knowing who is in the driver’s seat. They have approached the cars and sometimes used violence or threats to get people out, which experts say is contrary to best practices for policing.

The Trump administration’s push for thousands of deportations a day across the country has transformed the way ICE works. For months, advocates and community members in Maine have noted ICE sometimes using aggressive tactics, culminating in Guerrero’s killing. It put these tactics under such an intense microscope that shortly after the shooting, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin tried to pause vehicle stops but was overruled by President Donald Trump.

Chatterjee said the account his client gives of his arrest differs from ICE’s account. ICE said, in a document reviewed by the Portland Press Herald, that agents checked the driver’s identity before they took him into custody. Chatterjee’s client said they told him to get out of the car and restrained him and then checked his paperwork.

Like Guerrero, he is a father without a criminal record.

Tom Homan, Trump’s border czar, said on CNN on Sunday that a new policy mandates that for all vehicle stops, at least one body camera will record the event. It’s unclear how that will happen in Maine, given that ICE said it would take 60 days to deploy cameras to the half of field offices nationwide that don’t have them. Homan also said “journeymen” agents will be assigned to vehicle stops.

In another arrest this year, on Feb. 27, which does not appear to have involved Brouillette, Karl Goma was outside the four-unit building where he lived in Biddeford, just around the corner from where Guerrero was shot. ICE agents pulled up beside his car and told him to get out.

Goma had been working and paying rent, said the property manager, Ashanti Blok. His upstairs neighbor, Sierra, who asked to be referred to by her first name to protect her privacy, used her phone to film the first part of the interaction with ICE.

The video, which the Press Herald reviewed, showed three agents in vests at the car window. In a calm voice, one agent said “I’m going to have to break the window, and I’m going to have to pull you out.” Then he asked Goma again to step out of the car.

Sierra stopped filming in order to call Biddeford Police. She said she heard Goma’s daughters screaming “Don’t take my dad,” and she saw the agents smash the car window and drag Goma out of the car.

“He was wiggling around, not giving them the easiest of time, but he wasn’t resisting,” she said in an interview. Blok said it was “unnecessary” to smash the window, and “traumatic” for Goma’s wife and daughters to watch. While Goma was in custody, he and his family decided to leave the U.S., Blok said.

Chatterjee said he had never seen ICE agents smash car windows before Trump returned to office. His law firm is based in Massachusetts and regularly has clients who are detained in Maine and held in a detention facility in Plymouth, Massachusetts. Based on his firm’s cases, he believes ICE has used more aggressive tactics particularly since the January surge operation in Maine.

“It used to be more isolated incidents, but now I’d say it’s a pattern,” he said.

It’s not a universal experience, though. Attorneys at Haven Immigration Law in Portland, which also regularly represents people detained by ICE in Maine, said their clients have been taken into custody without conflict, though the firm has shown in court that many of its clients shouldn’t have been detained.

Chatterjee said the immigrants he represents who have reported getting threatened by ICE have no criminal history.

“They weren’t trying to avoid detection by immigration and most of them had work permits,” he said.

ICE and Trump have said vehicle stops are a necessary tool in the administration’s deportation efforts, but there are other ways to make these kinds of arrests, experts said.

Marc Brown, academic director and lead instructor at the Excellence in Policing and Public Safety Program at the University of South Carolina, called the tactic ICE is using a “vehicle takedown,” and contrasted it with a traffic stop. He said if other law enforcement agencies take down people in cars, they do a lot of coordination and planning.

It’s better practice to wait until a subject gets out of the car to try to engage them, he said. Avoiding a pursuit in a car is safer for the agents, the subject and bystanders, he added.

“Smashing the window, to me, creates more danger, because now you’re dealing with broken glass and potential for your suspect and the officer to be cut,” Brown said. Afterward, you still have to open the door, he said, so it doesn’t really give officers an advantage. He said even if police officers were pursuing a violent criminal, they would try to get the person out of the car a different way.

Immigrants targeted by ICE in Maine this year have often been accused of civil offenses, not crimes, and judges have ordered dozens of them released on bond.

Brown, who is also a former police officer and worked for the Federal Law Enforcement Training Centers where ICE agents get trained, said in his law enforcement career, even when there was an arrest warrant for someone, a first step might be to call them and ask them to turn themselves in. Overall, he said ICE could operate with more precision.

Deborah Ramirez, a former federal prosecutor who worked with the Drug Enforcement Administration and Federal Bureau of Investigation, agreed.

“They have to have probable cause to stop someone, and use only the amount of force that’s necessary,” said Ramirez, now a law professor at Northeastern University in Boston.

“Everyday the FBI arrests people,” she said. “Do they arrest people like this? No.”

Talking about instances where ICE has smashed windows, pulled people out of cars and detained people who were not the targets, she said, “That’s not the way you stop a car, especially if you’re in an unmarked car. Tactics matter.”

She said federal agents are trained not to shoot at a moving car. Officers should identify themselves, explain why they’re pulling someone over, and look at their identification, she said.

“The way they’re policing is dangerous to the community,” Ramirez said. She’s leading an effort to help cities and states hold ICE agents accountable in those incidents.

Brown said when he was an officer, ICE detained people who were already in jails, but were not in the streets.

“I don’t think they were designed to do this, so it’s not too surprising that they’re having some of the challenges that they’re having,” he said.

Ramirez, Brown and other experts say judicial warrants signed by a judge would be more effective, though they would add an administrative burden for the Trump administration and could slow the mass deportation effort.

Brown believes ICE’s public safety mission is being lost.

“If you’re not trying to ensure public safety,” he said, “then what are you doing?”

name: Human Rights
title: Nursing Mother of Two Arrested Without Warrant by ICE, Held 700 Miles From Her Children ...
description:
Ms. Perez is mother to a ten-month-old, whom she is breastfeeding, and a two-year-old with Down syndrome.
Ms. Perez is seeking asylum from Guatemala as a survivor of severe domestic violence.
Why would ICE violate its own rules just to target a nursing mother who has followed all the legal steps of the immigration system?
Advocacy and Litigation at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center.
ICE must release Maria and ensure she is back with her children, and stop wreaking havoc in our communities.” * Pseudonym used to protect the client’s safety
text:
JOINT PRESS RELEASE FROM: SANCTUARY OF THE SOUTH, TENNESSEE IMMIGRANT & REFUGEE RIGHTS COALITION, THE ACLU OF LOUISANA, THE ROBERT & ETHEL KENNEDY HUMAN RIGHTS CENTER AND AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL USA

Ms. Maria Perez* was arrested without a warrant by ICE while taking both of her children to the doctor. Ms. Perez is mother to a ten-month-old, whom she is breastfeeding, and a two-year-old with Down syndrome. Her arrest violates ICE’s own Directive 11032.4, which states that the agency should not “detain, arrest, or continue to detain individuals known to be pregnant, postpartum or nursing” except under exceptional circumstances.

Ms. Perez is now at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, nearly seven hundred miles away from her infant daughter and special needs toddler, who requires intensive, ongoing medical treatment and therapy for multiple health complications. With their mother forcibly removed, the children have missed their critical medical appointments and are now in the care of a neighbor, as Ms. Perez has no other support network in the area. She is currently suffering the physical effects of suddenly being unable to nurse, made worse by diabetes, which she had been actively managing before she was detained.

Ms. Perez is seeking asylum from Guatemala as a survivor of severe domestic violence. She has no criminal history and has complied with every requirement in the immigration process since entering the United States in 2022.

Sanctuary of the South (SOS) and Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition (TIRRC), Ms. Argueta’s legal counsel, have partnered with the ACLU of Louisiana, the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, and Amnesty International to submit a formal complaint to the Department of Homeland Security, urging the immediate release of Ms. Perez, and reiterating a commitment to pursuing all legal avenues to reunite her with her children, and seek relief for the profound harm the family has suffered as a result of their separation.

“SOS denounces the cruelty and complete lack of humanity in ICE’s decision to separate mother from children, especially nursing mothers from babies at such a tender age,” said Katie Blankenship, founder and managing attorney at SOS. “Being held in detention threatens Maria’s right to due process and is an unnecessary act of violence towards an immigrant mother and survivor of domestic violence. Families across the country share similar traumatic stories. We condemn family separation by ICE and demand Ms. Perez’s immediate release, so she may return to her children who so desperately need her.”

Spring Miller, Senior Director of Legal Strategy at TIRRC, added: “ICE and DHS continue to show blatant disregard not just for their own policies but for basic humanity. Ripping a nursing mother from her vulnerable children and shipping her to another state is almost unimaginable, yet ICE has turned a blind eye to their own directives and has done just that to Maria. Her case demonstrates the extraordinary cruelty these agencies inflict on people every day, and the multiple points at which people in detention are denied access to due process. We demand the immediate release of Ms. Perez to her children and condemn the countless ways ICE and DHS continue to separate families across the country.”

Ms. Perez’s case has drawn condemnation from major human rights and civil liberties organizations across the country, who have joined SOS and TIRRC in demanding her immediate release.

“The government’s continued torture of women is patently outrageous,” said Nora Ahmed, legal director for the ACLU of Louisiana. “Every person who claims to care about family values in this nation should be up in arms over these atrocious abuses. Why would ICE violate its own rules just to target a nursing mother who has followed all the legal steps of the immigration system? ICE has destroyed a family in the process and is directly responsible for putting children’s lives at risk. Everyone, regardless of political beliefs, should be outraged on behalf of Ms. Perez.”

“ICE snatched Maria from her nursing baby and shipped her to a detention center hundreds of miles from home,” said Anthony Enriquez, VP of U.S. Advocacy and Litigation at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center. “This cruel and degrading treatment of new mothers and pregnant women has been repeated hundreds of times over the last two years. We call on ICE to immediately release Maria.”

“To have your children taken from you is a parent’s worst nightmare,” said Amy Fischer, Director for Refugee and Migrant Rights, Amnesty International USA. “That’s what ICE agents did when they took Maria’s children from her, traumatizing all of them. Maria is still nursing her two children, one of whom has special needs. What ICE is doing in communities throughout the U.S. is cruel, inhumane, pointless, and against the law. Maria, and all parents, should be able to care for their children and go about their daily lives without fear of being forcibly separated. This cruelty must end. ICE must release Maria and ensure she is back with her children, and stop wreaking havoc in our communities.”

text:
A Japanese American-led coalition of residents, elected officials and faith leaders is speaking out against the Trump administration’s deadly immigration enforcement campaign and opposing a planned Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in Santa Clara County.

Members of the group said Wednesday the actions against immigrants and their families playing out in the nation today reflect the racist, white supremacist and unjust policies of the past, including when Japanese Americans were incarcerated based on their race during World War II.

“When you see your government begin to sort human beings into categories of who deserves rights and who doesn’t, who gets due process and who doesn’t, you do not stay quiet,” Rev. John Oda of the Wesley United Methodist Church said at a rally in San José’s Japantown.

His uncle fought and died for the United States during the war, while his family was locked away at the Heart Mountain American concentration camp in Wyoming, Oda said.

“You especially do not stay quiet when you have been taught via painful history exactly where that road leads,” he said.

Susan Hayase helped advance the movement for redress and reparations for Japanese Americans in the 1970s and 1980s, and co-founded San José Nikkei Resisters, a social justice organization.

“One of the things that former incarcerees like my parents’ generation and older told us is that they wanted to make sure that it would never happen to anybody else. And we took that as kind of a mission statement, kind of a command that was so important to us,” Hayase said in an interview.

The groups were joined by elected officials from local, county, state and federal offices, including Rep. Zoe Lofgren, State Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, Assemblymembers Ash Kalra and Patrick Ahrens, Santa Clara County Supervisor Betty Duong and San José City Councilmember Anthony Tordillos.

“ICE is out of control. It needs to be rebuilt from top to bottom. We have dangerous, masked, armed men snatching people who’ve lived here for years and disappearing them off the streets,” Lofgren said.

“And if that detention center is opened…what it’s going to mean is that those masked, armed, dangerous agents can fan out across Northern California and bring their reign of terror to our communities. We cannot allow that to happen,” she said.

In recent court filings, ICE agreed to voluntarily hold off on further construction of the facility as part of a scheduling compromise with attorneys for Santa Clara County and the Attorney General’s office.

The county and the state are also asking a judge for a preliminary injunction to halt the project indefinitely while the long-term litigation plays out.

The federal court hearing addressing the preliminary injunction is set for Sept. 8.

Lofgren expressed hope the lawsuit will prevail, but added that “we need to stand ready to do what else is necessary should those efforts fail.”

Hayase said she is very hopeful rallies and community-led actions will make real change, and she hopes others are inspired to take up such work, even if they haven’t been directly affected by the current policies.

“Sometimes people get used to bad news. They become calloused. But I think deep down inside, nobody wants violations of human rights to be happening in the United States,” she said.

“To make this system work, everybody has to participate,” she said. “You have to stand up for your own rights. But if you see somebody else’s rights being violated, you have to participate. And I think people aren’t used to that, but I think they can get used to it.”

description:
