text:
The Trump administration, for over a year, has chipped away at immigrants' ability to claim asylum, undercutting one of the few remaining ways for people fleeing persecution to stay in the U.S.

In the latest change this week, asylum officers could send hundreds of thousands more asylum applications to immigration courts. As a result, more asylum seekers are expected to be denied legal permission to stay in the country.

The rule affects applications filed at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), the branch of the Homeland Security Department that oversees legal migration. It comes as the administration has narrowed the scope of how someone can claim asylum or be approved for it, and curbed freedoms and benefits for those waiting for an answer. Asylum approvals are now at their lowest in at least two decades.

The changes come even as hundreds of thousands of TPS or temporary protected status holders are poised to lose the legal ability to work and live in the U.S. and are seeking additional avenues to stay, including asylum. And various other humanitarian programs like refugee resettlement and visas have been limited or paused.

"It's almost like a war on asylum," said Ruby Powers, an immigration attorney in Texas who represents asylum applicants across the country in immigration court and with USCIS. She has represented people from over 43 different countries.

"All of these individuals are trying to open up, share the traumatic events of where they were persecuted or have a future, and have a fair and honest review of their matter. But the rules have changed and very few are going to see approvals," she said.

President Trump's focus on immigration enforcement was clear when he returned to the White House last year: within hours of taking office, he declared a national emergency over what he described as an invasion at the southern border and shut down the cell phone application immigrants used to schedule asylum appointments.

Since then, officials have used the immigration court system, a sprawling arrest and deportation mandate and new congressional statutes to detain, deport and cut benefits for thousands of people who have claimed they are afraid to returning to their home countries for fear of persecution.

The new USCISrule would let asylum officers refer an asylum application to the immigration court system within the Justice Department, where attorneys say it is now likely to get rejected. The rule takes effect immediately, even as the agency collects public comments. It's meant to reduce the one-million case backlog at USCIS by about 30%.

The White House declined to comment on its approach to asylum. Officials at USCIS have defended the changes, saying the Biden administration made it too easy to get asylum.

"For far too long the asylum system has been exploited for purposes of delay and work authorization, not legitimate claims of protection," USCIS Director Joseph Edlow said in a statement about the latest rule. "America's asylum system exists to protect individuals who genuinely fear persecution and this rule will help ensure that resources are directed to the timely adjudication of those claims instead of to those seeking to use the system as a loophole."

Harder to apply for asylum at USCIS

Immigrants can apply for asylum at USCIS. They can only do so if they are already physically present in the U.S. — unlike refugees, who apply for the refugee program from abroad. Asylees need to prove a fear of returning to their home country based on one of five protected characteristics: race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion.

They have to apply within a year of arriving in the country, with some exceptions.

"It is difficult to get," Victoria Neilson, supervising attorney at the National Immigration Project, a legal advocacy group, said about the current status of the program. "The US-Mexico border is almost 'closed.' It's very difficult for anybody to get into the United States and seek asylum in that way."

She noted anyone who arrives by plane could file for asylum, as could those already here. That could open the door for thousands of people who are losing their temporary protected status to apply for asylum and request exceptions to the one-year rule.

There are more than 1 million pending asylum applications at USCIS, and another couple million at immigration courts. The agency paused the review of all applications for several months over the winter, leaving thousands of applicants in limbo. Lawyers said they had clients detained while attending their asylum interviews at USCIS.

"Before, with an asylum pending, you were protected and waited for your day to present your case. But now it's as if there is no protection," Powers, the Texas immigration attorney, said.

Powers said her office has been filing hundreds of asylum applications, including several hundred successfully for Afghan applicants, for example, but has received a higher level of denials under Trump than during past administrations.

"I could probably count on one hand how many approvals we've gotten from the asylum office this year and we're halfway through the year. That's very unheard of," she said. "We normally have a lot of approvals and we're not seeing that with the same quality of case types."

Harder to get asylum approved in immigration courts

Powers' reporting of an increase in asylum denials is not unique.

According to federal data analyzed by the group Mobile Pathways, the immigration court system is granting asylum at the lowest rates over the last two decades. The nonprofit tracks immigration court data and decisions.

The administration has touted the declining approval rate for asylum applications in immigration courts, pointing to its actions to terminate over 170 judges and hire others who are making rulings more in line with the administration's priorities.

"President Trump took decisive action, replacing activist judges — who slow-walked deportations and granted asylum at sky-high rates — with professionals committed to enforcing the law, not undermining it," according to a press release from April. "President Trump promised to end the open borders nightmare — and he is delivering on that promise with unrelenting force."

The decisions have aimed to cut the backlog of cases — though there are still some 2.4 million pending asylum applications, according to the Justice Department.

"Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration," said a DOJ spokesperson in a statement to NPR. "The Justice Department is restoring integrity to our immigration system by hearing cases fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly, in accordance with the law."

Matt Joseph spent 12 years at the Department of Homeland Security, including as an asylum officer. He says USCIS has always faced huge pressure to reduce the mounting backlog of cases, but hasn't received the resources.

"One persistent issue that's only gotten worse with time is the pressure to complete cases that literally have life-and-death stakes," Joseph said. "And there's a constant under-resourcing of the asylum office both in terms of personnel and other resources to get through these caseloads in an efficient manner."

Past administrations have also sought to curb asylum applications — including an Obama-era policy known as metering, which allowed border patrol agents to turn away people before they could physically enter the U.S. to claim asylum. The practice was expanded during Trump's first term, and the Supreme Court in June upheld the policy — though the ability to enter and claim asylum at the southern border was already largely limited.

Joseph left the agency last spring and now works as senior policy counsel at the Center for Gender and Refugee Studies, an advocacy and legal group that defends refugee rights. He said this administration's policies to limit asylum go beyond what past presidents have done.

"What you're really seeing is a concerted attack on asylum from all fronts by the administration," Joseph said. "They're really trying to keep people out of the asylum process to begin with. And if they are already in, they are trying to find a way to take people out of it."

Harder to appeal a decision

Immigrants whose applications are denied have a chance to appeal or seek other ways to avoid getting deported.

Appeals made in immigration court go to an administrative panel called the Board of Immigration Appeals, which is made up nearly entirely of Trump appointees. Under this administration, the board has issued a record number of precedent-setting decisions — about a third that limit or change the interpretation of asylum.

The asylum-related decisions issued by the BIA vary in scope. Some encourage third-country deportations. Others add additional scrutiny around claims of violence and persecution.

There have also been restrictions on the definitions around protected classes to make it harder to grant asylum around gender-based claims, the geography of the country and politically-based claims. Many of the BIA judges in their decisions bring up alleged civil and criminal infractions as a reason to not grant asylum and the consequences of new asylum fees.

"Part of the base strategy [is] to just pile up so many losses that it's hard for non-citizens to even argue that they merit a hearing before the immigration judge," said Neilson, from the National Immigration Project.

Life gets harder while waiting

Other policy changes across the federal government have made it harder for asylum seekers to live in the U.S.

A bill congressional Republicans passed last summer, for the first time imposed fees for asylum applications. It also added a fee for work authorization applications, and a yearly fee for each year an asylum application is pending. Such fees could total thousands of dollars for immigrants and their families waiting in limbo for years.

The legislation also stripped eligibility for asylum applicants and recipients to get benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and healthcare programs.

Separately, a newly proposed regulation from DHS would make asylum seekers wait for a longer period of time — for a year, up from five months — to apply for a work permit. The rule would also pause the processing of new work permits until USCIS reduces its asylum backlog.

Advocates warn the rule could result in more denials for people seeking to renew their work permits, risking the status of more than 2 million people already in the labor force.

Conchita Cruz, co-executive director of The Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, said the group has members who can't work legally because it has taken over a year to process their work permit renewals.

"Making it so that individuals have no ability to support themselves or their family does make it a lot harder to seek asylum," Cruz said.

DHS has also proposed another rule that would require additional biometric screening for people seeking a work permit, which advocates said could cause further delays in renewals, and bar those who have been arrested and not convicted from renewing their permits.

Despite all the changes aimed at discouraging asylum applicants from staying in the U.S., advocates like Cruz said it's unlikely many will leave the U.S.

"Asylum seekers don't have a choice. If they're safe here, they're likely going to stay here rather than risk their lives" by going back to their home country, Cruz said.

text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. — Gov. Gavin Newsom said Wednesday that newly-released federal court documents, including sworn deposition testimony and internal text messages from Homeland Security personnel, support his longstanding claim that a 2025 immigration enforcement operation outside one of his political rallies was driven by politics rather than legitimate public safety concerns.

The documents, filed as exhibits in ongoing federal litigation challenging Southern California immigration enforcement operations, include testimony from a Homeland Security Investigations special agent who described the operation outside Newsom’s event as lacking a legitimate operational purpose and appearing to be “purely political.” The case, Pedro Vasquez Perdomo et al. v. Markwayne Mullin et al., remains pending in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.

On Aug. 14, 2025, U.S. Border Patrol agents conducted an immigration enforcement operation outside Newsom’s Election Rigging Response Act rally in Little Tokyo, detaining “at least one person,” according to NBC Los Angeles.

The enforcement action drew immediate criticism from Newsom, who argued at the time that federal immigration authorities had intentionally targeted his political event at the direction of the Trump administration.

Nearly a year later, internal communications and sworn deposition testimony produced during discovery have become public, providing new details about how some federal agents viewed the operation.

“[Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents] marched to a Democratic governor’s press conference,” one Homeland Security Investigations agent said during a deposition, according to the Governor’s Office. “It seemed to be purely political. It did not seem like there was a good operational basis to be doing that.”

In the same deposition, the agent testified that the Aug. 14 raid was one of the “straws that broke the camel’s back” after confirming a text message in which he expressed hope that he would “be replaced soon.”

“I mean, the Home Depot was like being put in a position to potentially violate a Temporary Restraining Order,” the agent testified. “Then [the raid] was just, I thought, ridiculous.”

According to the deposition, the agent had previously voiced concerns about immigration operations conducted at Home Depot parking lots, where he believed agents risked detaining individuals who were not the intended targets of enforcement actions. He testified that the operations became “less and less targeted” over time and expressed concern that agents increasingly pursued people who fled after seeing law enforcement rather than focusing exclusively on individuals identified in advance.

The deposition also contrasts the agent’s prior experience as a Border Patrol agent near the U.S.-Mexico border with the 2025 urban enforcement operations in Los Angeles. The agent testified that traditional Border Patrol operations generally occurred close to the border in controlled environments, while the Los Angeles operations involved densely populated urban areas where distinguishing targeted individuals from bystanders was more difficult.

In several text messages cited by the Governor’s Office, agents referred to the operation as “purely political.” Another exchange indicates agents were pulled away from enforcement activity at a Home Depot and a nearby car wash to “run this stunt,” referring to the raid outside Newsom’s event.

“We were told to assist with targeted enforcement,” one message from an agent reads. “That is not target[ed] enforcement. That was just a political agenda.”

According to the Governor’s Office, the court filings contradict the Trump administration’s repeated assertions that immigration enforcement operations were focused on removing dangerous criminals.

“The evidence tells a different story,” the Governor’s Office said. “Their strategy has become one of dangerous quotas over public safety and headlines over results.”

The Governor’s Office said the documents also describe what it characterized as the broader consequences of the administration’s immigration enforcement strategy, arguing that current practices have resulted in wrongful detentions, family separations, wrongful deportations and economic harm to California businesses.

In addition to messages concerning the political nature of the Aug. 14 operation, the court documents include what the Governor’s Office described as “deeply offensive racist remarks exchanged by some agents,” including slurs directed at Latinos and immigrants.

“The same records depict an enforcement strategy driven by politics, indiscriminate sweeps and a dehumanizing attitude toward the people caught in them,” the statement said.

Newsom said the newly-released documents demonstrate an abuse of federal authority and accused the Trump administration of diverting immigration enforcement resources to advance political objectives rather than public safety.

“The federal government should never be used as a weapon against political opponents or their families,” Newsom said, according to the Governor’s Office. “This is an abuse of power, and every American, regardless of party, should be deeply concerned.”

The announcement notes that Newsom has previously accused the Trump administration of politically targeting him, including by seeking records from the Department of Justice related to federal investigations involving the governor and members of his family.

The text messages and deposition testimony became public after they were filed as exhibits in the ongoing federal lawsuit challenging the legality of the 2025 immigration enforcement operations. The litigation remains pending, and the allegations reflected in the filings have not yet been adjudicated by the court.

text:
This is a web edition of GBH Daily, a weekday newsletter bringing you local stories you can trust so you can stay informed without feeling overwhelmed.

Sign up here!

☔A rainy, foggy day with highs in the 70s. Sunset is at 8:05 p.m.

Last year, Department of Defense officials said they planned to assign as many as 600 active-duty military members as temporary immigration judges. The Trump administration has fired or terminated the employment of about 100 immigration judges nationwide, meaning the already slow system is now even slower as immigrants await rulings on asylum cases, bail and deportation.

So who are these active duty troops serving as judges, what are their qualifications and how did they get assigned? The ACLU of Massachusetts is suing to try to find out.

“There is reason to believe, however, that in fact, that these are not merely lawyers who happen to be military reservists who are being hired in their civilian capacity to be temporary immigration judges,” Dan McFadden, managing attorney of the ACLU of Massachusetts, told GBH’s Sarah Betancourt. “But in fact, they’re being activated on active duty orders through the Department of Defense and ordered to operate as temporary immigration judges. That raises a lot of very serious legal questions.” You can read more about the program and the lawsuit here.

Four Things to Know

1. Employers, many of them health care organizations, have laid off or placed on leave Haitian workers whose legal immigration protections were revoked after the Supreme Court ruled that the Trump administration could end Temporary Protected Status for Haitians and Syrians. That includes about 1,500 workers in nursing facilities, an industry already struggling to attract workers.

“We work with some of the most vulnerable individuals in the state, and having compassionate care with staff who have worked with these individuals for extended periods of time is so vitally important to the services we provide,” said Michelle Fraser, director of employee relations at Vinfen. “By having this disruption, it does potentially impact the continuity and the quality of care that we provide.”

2. With the formal end of the state’s legislative session coming tomorrow — though that deadline isn’t quite so final this year under new rules lawmakers set for themselves — Gov. Maura Healey said she wants to see the Legislature pass a bill that would ban federal immigration agents from making arrests in Massachusetts courthouses. The bill is called the PROTECT Act, and lawmakers have said they’re expecting to pass it this week.

“It’s about protecting our residents, protecting our communities in the face of unbelievable, unconstitutional, and what I think is un-American actions out of the Trump administration,” Healey told GBH’s Boston Public Radio yesterday.

3. Engineers and business leaders in Boston are talking about how they could use thermal energy from local waterways to heat and cool buildings. Their goal is to start with universities, hospitals and other big institutions. GBH’s Craig LeMoultwrote about the technical details of a similar project here.

“We see them as potential customers of this future system. And so we want to bring them along with us as we design this project,” said Lindsay Butler, executive director of the Green Ribbon Commission. “We want something that’s technically feasible, economically feasible and feasible from a regulatory and permitting perspective. But we also want something that’s going to work for the large institutions.”

4. Public health officials in Massachusetts don’t believe the 18 cases of the parasitic gastrointestinal illness Cyclospora recorded here this year are related to the larger national outbreak. But Public Health Commissioner Dr. Robbie Goldstein said he’d like people to pay attention to where their produce comes from.

“What’s being recalled? Where did you go shopping? What’s on your shelves and what might you want to take off your shelves and maybe throw away and not use?” he told GBH’s Morning Edition. “We know as the temperature gets warmer through August and the beginning of September, cyclospora can still persist, and then it usually goes away into the fall.”

What an acclaimed translator of ‘The Odyssey’ thinks about Christopher Nolan’s new film

Have you seen Christopher Nolan’s new film adaptation of “The Odyssey,” or at least enjoyed the memes about Matt Damon as Boston Odysseus? Emily Wilson, whose 2017 translation of Homer’s epic inspired Nolan’s adaptation, spoke to Culture Show host Jared Bowen about the story. Their conversation explored translation: converting an ancient Greek poem into English, how humans in the story understand the language of the gods and adapting the story from page to an IMAX screen.

“For any literary translator, you have to think through: which elements of the original work of literature, poetry or prose do I most want to convey, and how can I do that with this impossible challenge of, use not of the same words and yet have it be exactly the same?” Wilson said. She wrote her translation in iambic pentameter to try to preserve the feeling people would have had listening to a performance of “The Odyssey” in ancient Greek.

Wilson said she thinks Nolan’s film is “an amazing spectacle at the movies,” especially on giant IMAX screens. “In terms of the script, I was disappointed by it. I just felt that there were so many wonderful actors who weren’t given enough to do,” she said. “I just didn’t think there was enough complexity.”

text:
Passengers checking in for domestic flights are increasingly finding themselves at the center of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement has begun arresting some travelers at U.S. airports, according to reports from The New York Times and ABC News, marking a new front in the administration's push to boost deportations and reach its target of 2,000 immigration arrests per day.

The arrests come as a newly disclosed agreement between the Transportation Security Administration and ICE is drawing scrutiny from immigration advocates and privacy groups. The memorandum, released July 28 by watchdog group American Oversight, outlines how TSA and ICE can share passenger information and how that data is stored and used.

At least 27 people have been arrested at airports for allegedly overstaying their visas, according to the reports. Immigration attorneys told ABC News that some people swept up in the enforcement effort have valid work authorization and no criminal history.

Why are ICE arrests happening at airports?

While ICE has long had the authority to detain people who are in the country unlawfully or who have final removal orders, immigration attorneys say the agency is now using airports in ways not commonly seen before.

"ICE is working with TSA and targeting people at check-in counters and gates, sidestepping the warrants and surveillance operations used in the past," Buffalo-based immigration attorney Rosanna Berardi told ABC News.

"There is no investigation or no home visit involved. It's simply a name match at a checkpoint, and that's what makes this approach so efficient for ICE and so unsettling for travelers."

The newly released TSA-ICE memorandum has fueled concerns that information travelers provide while flying could be used more broadly for immigration enforcement.

"Americans provide their personal information to board a plane safely, not to become part of an immigration enforcement system or a government surveillance network," American Oversight Executive Director Chioma Chukwu said in a statement.

Las Vegas airport incident put spotlight on tactic

The emerging enforcement strategy gained national attention earlier this month after a video recorded at Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas went viral online.

The footage showed a handcuffed man on the ground surrounded by two ICE agents in civilian clothes. After bystanders questioned the agents about what was happening, the agents left the area.

The Department of Homeland Security later identified the man as Phu Nguyen, an undocumented immigrant from Australia who was born in Vietnam.

DHS told Nevada Connect, part of the USA TODAY Network, that "As officers attempted to arrest Nguyen, a crowd of anti-ICE agitators surrounded officers. To de-escalate the situation and for officer safety, officers did not proceed with the arrest at the Las Vegas Airport and chose to instead arrest him at his flight the following day departing the Los Angeles International Airport on July 14."

What happens next?

The airport arrests signal how immigration enforcement is increasingly extending into everyday public spaces as the Trump administration intensifies its deportation efforts.

With ICE under pressure to increase arrest numbers and TSA passenger data now the subject of growing scrutiny, airports may become one of the most visible battlegrounds in the administration's broader immigration strategy.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to USA TODAY's request for comment on July 29.

Carly Sauvageau of Nevada Connect, part of the USA TODAY NETWORK contributed to this report.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

text:
Illinois elected officials in the Latino Caucus and allied advocates are seeking to connect families of people arrested at courthouses with civil rights attorneys for potential legal action, Democratic state Rep. Lilian Jimenez of Chicago said Wednesday.

The call for affected families came months after Illinois passed a law largely banning civil immigration enforcement against people involved in courthouse proceedings. It also coincided with an announcement that lawmakers in several other states are pursuing similar legislation that would make it easier for people to sue immigration enforcement agents, following Illinois’ lead.

“We want to make sure those laws are not just pieces of paper but they’re actually enforceable,” Jimenez said after the news conference.

Gov. JB Pritzker signed the measure in December 2025, banning federal agents from making certain arrests near courthouses and easing the path for people to sue if they think their rights were violated during civil immigration arrests.

Even with the law in place, immigration agents have continued to appear around Cook County courthouses, the Tribune has previously reported, citing a tracker maintained by the Cook County public defender’s office.

“We continue to make a call out for anybody who has been impacted. There are a number of organizations that are ready to support and file those lawsuits on behalf of those family members,” Jimenez said. Latino elected officials at the city, county and state levels, as well as groups including the Illinois Coalition for Immigrant and Refugee Rights, are leading the effort, she said, encouraging affected families to call the ICIRR hotline.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson previously called courthouse arrests “common sense.”

“It conserves valuable law enforcement resources because they already know where a target will be,” the DHS spokesperson said in a statement to the Tribune.

Rapid responders to immigration enforcement and state lawmakers have reported that Chicago saw an escalation in immigration enforcement in recent weeks.

Advocates argue that the presence of immigration agents can have a chilling effect on the criminal justice system, discouraging victims and defendants from participating in cases out of fear of arrest. Agents have been reported in or near the domestic violence courthouse at 555 W. Harrison St. at least 22 times since the beginning of the year, the Tribune noted earlier this month.

Lawmakers from states including Minnesota, Colorado and Utah gathered at a South Loop event space Wednesday as part of what they described as a nationwide push to pass legislation making it easier for their constituents to sue over constitutional violations by immigration agents, mirroring the law Illinois passed last year.

States including Vermont, Connecticut and Maryland have also passed similar laws, according to local news outlets.

Five initial lawsuits against immigration enforcement agents in Illinois were filed earlier this month, Democratic state Rep. Norma Hernandez of Melrose Park said.

“We are looking forward to more,” she said.

States have developed a “playbook” for introducing or passing such legislation nationwide, said EJ Juárez, executive director of the State Innovation Exchange, which aims to pass progressive state policies nationally.

“Federal law does not exempt you from the consequences of enacting violence and terror in communities in this country,” Juárez said.

authors: John Daley, Nicole Vap, John Daley Nicole Vap, Ava Kian, Alisha Sweeney, Molly Cruse, Outside Contributor, Orion Cenkl, Tom Hesse, Andrea Chalfin

Aurora’s statement called for GEO to fully cooperate with public health officials “to “determine the scope” of the TB situation at the GEO Aurora ICE Processing Center, and to ensure it’s not spreading.
Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman said it’s “simply a public health question,” not about immigration, and warned of litigation if there’s no compliance.

text:
Someone, maybe several people, had the highly contagious illness tuberculosis while in an Aurora immigration detention facility. That much is known. But beyond that, answers about who, how many, and where they are today have not been provided, while state, county and local governments point fingers of blame and the contractor that runs the facility simply refuses to cooperate with anyone outside of ICE.

The impasse revolves, at least in part, around whether companies like GEO, the group that has a federal contract to run the facility, has any obligation to follow state laws.

At stake is nothing less than the public's safety from tuberculosis or any other contagious disease that might develop in the facility.

State law requires the reporting of TB, and spells out various steps to contain its spread including statutes about investigation, lab results and medical records as well as penalties for violations of health orders.

GEO Group, a publicly traded company based in Florida, declined comment. It referred questions, as it has for weeks now, to ICE. However, in a lawsuit they filed against Colorado last month, GEO claimed it didn’t have to abide by a new state law requiring regular health and safety inspections of immigrant detention facilities because federal law reigns supreme.

Meanwhile, a July 17 deadline from the state health department for GEO to comply and provide “immediate cooperation” is now long past, with no cooperation.

WIRED magazine reported Wednesday that ICE has proposed new contracts that say state and local laws don’t apply to their detention centers. Those contracts have not been approved.

Aurora’s City Council added its voice to the chorus Monday, urging the operator of an immigration detection center to cooperate with a public health investigation into a confirmed case of tuberculosis. That demand has not been met by those in charge of the facility.

Aurora’s statement called for GEO to fully cooperate with public health officials “to “determine the scope” of the TB situation at the GEO Aurora ICE Processing Center, and to ensure it’s not spreading. Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman said it’s “simply a public health question,” not about immigration, and warned of litigation if there’s no compliance.

CPR reached out to GEO and to ICE Wednesday asking for them to respond to Aurora’s demands. GEO referred CPR to ICE. An unnamed ICE spokesperson responded with an answer that was a virtual carbon copy of one sent to CPR last week. The facility, they said, doesn’t have “any confirmed active tuberculosis (TB) cases.” It did have one June 25, and the person was “treated, cleared and removed.”

Aurora Mayor Mike Coffman thinks the next step in the stalemate could be litigation. “I think there is going to be litigation on this issue, if there's no compliance,” he said during a Monday’s meeting of the Aurora City Council where they demanded that GEO cooperate with public health authorities.

But litigation against the federal government or a multi-national corporation with government contracts could be time consuming and costly. Right now, since Adams County Health Department is the only agency that has filed a public health order, only Adams County would seemingly have jurisdiction to file suit.

The Colorado Attorney General’s office told CPR in order for it to take on a suit like that the Colorado Department of Health and Environment would need to issue a public health order.

Why hasn't CDPHE done that? A CDPHE spokeswoman said “rather than duplicating steps that have already been taken, at this time, we continue to seek avenues we can take to break this impasse.” She noted both Adams County and the state “continue to be stonewalled by the facility.”

A Colorado advocacy coalition called Shut Down GEO, sent out an email blast urging people to call the director of the state health department to urge her to issue a state public health order, which would increase the state’s options “to hold GEO accountable through fines or lawsuits.”

As the standoff goes on, those who were detained at the center have few answers as to their personal vulnerability to tuberculosis. News that ICE had a confirmed case inside the facility came as a surprise to those who were most immediately affected - those detained inside.

“They were afraid that they were going to catch illnesses that they weren't even aware about,” said Andrea Loya, executive director of Casa de Paz, a non-profit immigrant advocacy group.

Some detainees, since released, told her they first learned of the case of the highly infectious disease not from facility staff, but by following news coverage from inside the center.

“Some people found out on the news,” she said.

The Guardian reported earlier this month that the outbreak had hit at least a dozen detainees, based on the account of a detainee inside. Without compliance with public health authorities, there is no way to know if others in the facility were put at risk.

Loya described the stalemate, lack of information about prevention efforts and GEO’s apparent defiance of state law, alarming. “If it's not tuberculosis that gets the alarms ringing, then what is it going to be?” she said.

U.S. Rep. Jason Crow, a Democrat who represents Aurora, said “GEO and ICE continue to stonewall both state and county health authorities, not allowing them access to the facility, which frankly is an abomination.”

His staff has been doing regular site visits and routinely gotten some basic information. But that’s changed in recent weeks. “They've shut off the ability of the local ICE and GEO folks answering our questions when we're doing these visits and have centralized all of it to national ICE in DC,” Crow said in an interview on Friday.

Why it matters to public health

Experts say the kind of investigation outlined in state law is needed because of how serious the disease is.

Anytime TB is detected in a setting where a lot of people live it’s dangerous.

TB is an airborne bacterial lung infection. It’s contagious. It thrives in crowded, poorly ventilated places–places like detention centers, where it can spread, among detainees, among staff, and from them potentially to people outside.

“Tuberculosis can be very infectious and can be quite transmissible, especially in areas where there's dense populations or a dense amount of people,” said UCHealth infectious-disease specialist Dr. Michelle Barron. “So it's something obviously that is of concern from a public health standpoint.”

TB is curable, but if untreated it can be fatal. That’s why states have laws about TB and why public health authorities take it seriously.

“Tuberculosis is very treatable. We have good drugs,” Barron said. “It grows very slowly. So the onset of it, it can be over months. It's not typically something that suddenly occurs. And in that timeframe, people can be quite infectious.”

And if someone catches TB and it’s not treated, it can develop into latent TB. About 5% who have been infected develop TB disease in the first two years after infection; another 5% will develop it later in life, according to the CDC.

Polis says GEO Group needs to provide “better information”

“We need better information,” Gov. Jared Polis told Colorado Matters host Ryan Warner in an interview Tuesday, four days following CPR’s first interview with him since reports of TB inside the GEO facility emerged.

Polis said GEO had a “fine relationship” with the Adams County Health Department until a month or two ago, when the TB case was first identified.

Polis said after the case made news, communication stopped.

“Then that communication line broke down. And so we are just trying to restart that communication line between Adams County and GEO,” he said.

The governor said it’s not so much about getting public health investigators into the facility, but about GEO showing what steps it’s taken to track and treat other potential cases.

“GEO said the person who might have been contagious has now either been treated or is out of the state. What about the five or 10 people (other people they may have exposed)?” Polis asked hypothetically. “What about their cellmate? How do we make sure in a month or two, if they were housed with somebody that person is tested?”

Then he asked about the employees, “How do we make sure that employees of GEO, these are Coloradans that work for that contract organization, how do we make sure they're tested in a few months to see whether they convert positive?”

The governor said county health departments are an extension of the state and communication needs to happen with any of these types of congregate facilities that house people.

“[GEO] needs to show the paper trail and the documentation of what was done and who was exposed,” Polis said. “They absolutely need to be engaged with their county health department to make sure that they're able to account for anybody that might be exposed in the facility, especially those that are going back out into the community.”

GEO Group’s perspective

GEO Group hasn’t answered any questions from CPR, or apparently anyone else. But the position of its legal team was revealed in a court case last month.

Last month the corporation, which operates the Aurora center plus immigrant detention facilities around the country, filed a lawsuit against the state to stop enforcement of a new law, signed by the governor, which requires regular health and safety inspections of immigrant detention facilities.

The corporation argued the law exceeded the state’s authority and “violates the supremacy clause” of the U.S. Constitution and also “impairs” GEO’s U.S. contracts, in violation of the Constitution, according to the lawsuit.

It states on its website that health staffing at the Aurora center is “more than double” that of correctional facilities in many states and access to off-site medical specialists, imaging facilities, emergency medical services, and community hospitals is available.

Note: CPR reporter Allison Sherry contributed to this story.

text:
JUANA SUMMERS, HOST:

There is new evidence that federal immigration agents in Los Angeles used derogatory and racial slurs to describe Latinos who they were targeting in recent immigration raids. The slurs are heard in body cam footage that is now a part of a federal lawsuit accusing ICE and Border Patrol agents of racial profiling as they search for immigrants to detain. NPR's Adrian Florido joins us now - and a note that we will hear some of those slurs in this segment. Hi, Adrian.

ADRIAN FLORIDO, BYLINE: Hi, Juana.

SUMMERS: So these body cam videos from immigration agents - tell us what they show.

FLORIDO: Well, the videos are from last year, and they show the agents carrying out the aggressive immigration raids that have become a hallmark of President Trump's deportation campaign. But these videos also capture agents' conversations inside their vehicles as they're driving around LA looking for people to arrest, and you hear them using slurs to talk about the people they're targeting.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #1: Jesus [expletive] Christ, dude. I think they did get quite a few.

FLORIDO: In this video, two agents are talking about an operation that has just finished.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #1: I checked one guy's ID.

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #2: Did you?

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #1: Yeah.

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #2: There was a guy. I'm pretty sure he was w**. He was just sitting in that minivan.

FLORIDO: He says, there was a guy - I'm pretty sure he was w** - just sitting in that minivan. And w**, Juana, is short for w**back, a racial slur for immigrants from Mexico. And listen to how these agents in a different video talk about someone they've just spotted in a car.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #3: There's one right there (laughter).

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #4: OK, gray Tahoe. (Inaudible).

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #3: It looked like a t**k in the driver's seat.

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #4: Probably was.

SUMMERS: Adrian, did I hear him there say t**k?

FLORIDO: Yeah, t**k is a term that immigration agents have been known to use for migrants. It refers to the sound of an agent's flashlight when it hits a migrant's head. In the past, Border Patrol supervisors have forbidden agents from using this term because it's derogatory. But t**k shows up several times in these body cam videos. In this video, two agents are speaking a - in a mix of Spanish and English, and they're celebrating having just gotten, quote, "a t**k."

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #5: Yeah, I got us un tonky (ph).

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #6: I did.

UNIDENTIFIED AGENT #5: (Inaudible). How do you turn off the camera? How do you turn off the camera?

FLORIDO: The man arrested in that operation was later released. He was a U.S. citizen.

SUMMERS: And how have these videos come to light?

FLORIDO: Well, a federal judge in Los Angeles ordered the government to turn agent body cam video and text messages over to the ACLU as part of its lawsuit against ICE and Border Patrol. Last summer, the ACLU and other groups sued alleging that agents are racially profiling, stopping and arresting people just because they look Latino. I spoke with Mayra Joachin, one of the ACLU's attorneys in this case.

MAYRA JOACHIN: We now know the only evidence that those agents used to stop an individual was to racially profile and to identify people on the street who appear to look Latino and working-class.

FLORIDO: The government has argued in court that its agents decide who to stop based on many factors and say they don't racially profile. But Joachin says these videos and other evidence that they've submitted in this case show that agents really are just choosing people who look Latino.

SUMMERS: Now, Adrian, if I recall correctly, this case did come before the Supreme Court last year, and the court's conservative majority sided with the Trump administration. Is that right?

FLORIDO: Yeah, that's right. The high court ruling lifted some temporary restrictions that the LA judge had placed on ICE and Border Patrol. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that agents are allowed to use race as one among other factors. That Supreme Court ruling, though, did not stop this lawsuit from moving forward. And the ACLU says these videos strengthen their case that race is the main factor agents are using, and they want the judge in LA to order agents to stop using race and to document why they are stopping people.

SUMMERS: And last thing, Adrian, how has the Trump administration responded to this new evidence?

FLORIDO: The Department of Homeland Security sent me a very short statement that said, in part, quote, "our agents are focused on protecting the American people, not entertaining performative outrage."

SUMMERS: NPR's Adrian Florido, thank you.

FLORIDO: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

title: The Trump administration has undercut the U.S. asylum program. These 3 charts show how - NPR
description:
In the latest change this week, asylum officers could send hundreds of thousands more asylum applications to immigration courts.
The new USCISrule would let asylum officers refer an asylum application to the immigration court system within the Justice Department, where attorneys say it is now likely to get rejected.
Harder to apply for asylum at USCIS Immigrants can apply for asylum at USCIS.
The decisions have aimed to cut the backlog of cases — though there are still some 2.4 million pending asylum applications, according to the Justice Department.
Appeals made in immigration court go to an administrative panel called the Board of Immigration Appeals, which is made up nearly entirely of Trump appointees.
text:
The Trump administration, for over a year, has chipped away at immigrants' ability to claim asylum, undercutting one of the few remaining ways for people fleeing persecution to stay in the U.S.

In the latest change this week, asylum officers could send hundreds of thousands more asylum applications to immigration courts. As a result, more asylum seekers are expected to be denied legal permission to stay in the country.

The rule affects applications filed at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), the branch of the Homeland Security Department that oversees legal migration. It comes as the administration has narrowed the scope of how someone can claim asylum or be approved for it, and curbed freedoms and benefits for those waiting for an answer. Asylum approvals are now at their lowest in at least two decades.

The changes come even as hundreds of thousands of TPS or temporary protected status holders are poised to lose the legal ability to work and live in the U.S. and are seeking additional avenues to stay, including asylum. And various other humanitarian programs like refugee resettlement and visas have been limited or paused.

"It's almost like a war on asylum," said Ruby Powers, an immigration attorney in Texas who represents asylum applicants across the country in immigration court and with USCIS. She has represented people from over 43 different countries.

"All of these individuals are trying to open up, share the traumatic events of where they were persecuted or have a future, and have a fair and honest review of their matter. But the rules have changed and very few are going to see approvals," she said.

President Trump's focus on immigration enforcement was clear when he returned to the White House last year: within hours of taking office, he declared a national emergency over what he described as an invasion at the southern border and shut down the cell phone application immigrants used to schedule asylum appointments.

Since then, officials have used the immigration court system, a sprawling arrest and deportation mandate and new congressional statutes to detain, deport and cut benefits for thousands of people who have claimed they are afraid to returning to their home countries for fear of persecution.

The new USCISrule would let asylum officers refer an asylum application to the immigration court system within the Justice Department, where attorneys say it is now likely to get rejected. The rule takes effect immediately, even as the agency collects public comments. It's meant to reduce the one-million case backlog at USCIS by about 30%.

The White House declined to comment on its approach to asylum. Officials at USCIS have defended the changes, saying the Biden administration made it too easy to get asylum.

"For far too long the asylum system has been exploited for purposes of delay and work authorization, not legitimate claims of protection," USCIS Director Joseph Edlow said in a statement about the latest rule. "America's asylum system exists to protect individuals who genuinely fear persecution and this rule will help ensure that resources are directed to the timely adjudication of those claims instead of to those seeking to use the system as a loophole."

Harder to apply for asylum at USCIS

Immigrants can apply for asylum at USCIS. They can only do so if they are already physically present in the U.S. — unlike refugees, who apply for the refugee program from abroad. Asylees need to prove a fear of returning to their home country based on one of five protected characteristics: race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion.

They have to apply within a year of arriving in the country, with some exceptions.

"It is difficult to get," Victoria Neilson, supervising attorney at the National Immigration Project, a legal advocacy group, said about the current status of the program. "The US-Mexico border is almost 'closed.' It's very difficult for anybody to get into the United States and seek asylum in that way."

She noted anyone who arrives by plane could file for asylum, as could those already here. That could open the door for thousands of people who are losing their temporary protected status to apply for asylum and request exceptions to the one-year rule.

There are more than 1 million pending asylum applications at USCIS, and another couple million at immigration courts. The agency paused the review of all applications for several months over the winter, leaving thousands of applicants in limbo. Lawyers said they had clients detained while attending their asylum interviews at USCIS.

"Before, with an asylum pending, you were protected and waited for your day to present your case. But now it's as if there is no protection," Powers, the Texas immigration attorney, said.

Powers said her office has been filing hundreds of asylum applications, including several hundred successfully for Afghan applicants, for example, but has received a higher level of denials under Trump than during past administrations.

"I could probably count on one hand how many approvals we've gotten from the asylum office this year and we're halfway through the year. That's very unheard of," she said. "We normally have a lot of approvals and we're not seeing that with the same quality of case types."

Harder to get asylum approved in immigration courts

Powers' reporting of an increase in asylum denials is not unique.

According to federal data analyzed by the group Mobile Pathways, the immigration court system is granting asylum at the lowest rates over the last two decades. The nonprofit tracks immigration court data and decisions.

The administration has touted the declining approval rate for asylum applications in immigration courts, pointing to its actions to terminate over 170 judges and hire others who are making rulings more in line with the administration's priorities.

"President Trump took decisive action, replacing activist judges — who slow-walked deportations and granted asylum at sky-high rates — with professionals committed to enforcing the law, not undermining it," according to a press release from April. "President Trump promised to end the open borders nightmare — and he is delivering on that promise with unrelenting force."

The decisions have aimed to cut the backlog of cases — though there are still some 2.4 million pending asylum applications, according to the Justice Department.

"Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration," said a DOJ spokesperson in a statement to NPR. "The Justice Department is restoring integrity to our immigration system by hearing cases fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly, in accordance with the law."

Matt Joseph spent 12 years at the Department of Homeland Security, including as an asylum officer. He says USCIS has always faced huge pressure to reduce the mounting backlog of cases, but hasn't received the resources.

"One persistent issue that's only gotten worse with time is the pressure to complete cases that literally have life-and-death stakes," Joseph said. "And there's a constant under-resourcing of the asylum office both in terms of personnel and other resources to get through these caseloads in an efficient manner."

Past administrations have also sought to curb asylum applications — including an Obama-era policy known as metering, which allowed border patrol agents to turn away people before they could physically enter the U.S. to claim asylum. The practice was expanded during Trump's first term, and the Supreme Court in June upheld the policy — though the ability to enter and claim asylum at the southern border was already largely limited.

Joseph left the agency last spring and now works as senior policy counsel at the Center for Gender and Refugee Studies, an advocacy and legal group that defends refugee rights. He said this administration's policies to limit asylum go beyond what past presidents have done.

"What you're really seeing is a concerted attack on asylum from all fronts by the administration," Joseph said. "They're really trying to keep people out of the asylum process to begin with. And if they are already in, they are trying to find a way to take people out of it."

Harder to appeal a decision

Immigrants whose applications are denied have a chance to appeal or seek other ways to avoid getting deported.

Appeals made in immigration court go to an administrative panel called the Board of Immigration Appeals, which is made up nearly entirely of Trump appointees. Under this administration, the board has issued a record number of precedent-setting decisions — about a third that limit or change the interpretation of asylum.

The asylum-related decisions issued by the BIA vary in scope. Some encourage third-country deportations. Others add additional scrutiny around claims of violence and persecution.

There have also been restrictions on the definitions around protected classes to make it harder to grant asylum around gender-based claims, the geography of the country and politically-based claims. Many of the BIA judges in their decisions bring up alleged civil and criminal infractions as a reason to not grant asylum and the consequences of new asylum fees.

"Part of the base strategy [is] to just pile up so many losses that it's hard for non-citizens to even argue that they merit a hearing before the immigration judge," said Neilson, from the National Immigration Project.

Life gets harder while waiting

Other policy changes across the federal government have made it harder for asylum seekers to live in the U.S.

A bill congressional Republicans passed last summer, for the first time imposed fees for asylum applications. It also added a fee for work authorization applications, and a yearly fee for each year an asylum application is pending. Such fees could total thousands of dollars for immigrants and their families waiting in limbo for years.

The legislation also stripped eligibility for asylum applicants and recipients to get benefits from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and healthcare programs.

Separately, a newly proposed regulation from DHS would make asylum seekers wait for a longer period of time — for a year, up from five months — to apply for a work permit. The rule would also pause the processing of new work permits until USCIS reduces its asylum backlog.

Advocates warn the rule could result in more denials for people seeking to renew their work permits, risking the status of more than 2 million people already in the labor force.

Conchita Cruz, co-executive director of The Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, said the group has members who can't work legally because it has taken over a year to process their work permit renewals.

"Making it so that individuals have no ability to support themselves or their family does make it a lot harder to seek asylum," Cruz said.

DHS has also proposed another rule that would require additional biometric screening for people seeking a work permit, which advocates said could cause further delays in renewals, and bar those who have been arrested and not convicted from renewing their permits.

Despite all the changes aimed at discouraging asylum applicants from staying in the U.S., advocates like Cruz said it's unlikely many will leave the U.S.

text:
More than 24,000 immigrant children who arrived in the U.S. without a parent or guardian and are facing deportation could lose access to legal representation this week when a federal contract funding nonprofit legal services expires, leaving some organizations to scale back or end assistance altogether.

The cuts are compounded by the Trump administration’s refusal to reimburse the nonprofits roughly $65 million for legal services they have already provided to unaccompanied migrant children — payments the organizations argue they are entitled to under federal law.

The expiration of the contract on Friday, legal providers said, will affect about 90 organizations nationwide, including several in California.

Lindsay Toczylowski, chief executive director and co-founder of the Immigrant Defenders Law Center, which serves 13 facilities in Greater Los Angeles, said during a Wednesday news conference that more than 1,500 unaccompanied children that her organization represents will be affected.

Toczylowski said other organizations in the L.A. area that will be affected include the Public Counsel, Central American Resource Center and the Immigration Center for Women and Children.

“I’m thinking of clients I personally have represented over the years — trafficking victims, asylum seekers, children separated from their parents — and wondering what chance kids like them will have if no one is there to fight for them,” she said. “Lawyers are often the only independent witnesses in the immigration system. ... [They] have been the ones to uncover abuse, document unlawful conditions, expose government failures, and ensure children’s rights are not being violated.”

Toczylowski said it was attorneys who filed legal petitions for two young girls — ages 6 and 15 — to reunite them with their families after they had languished in federal custody for some seven months.

Elsewhere in the country, some organizations say they’re being forced to end legal services for unaccompanied children.

That’s the case for Melissa Lopez of Estrella El Paso, a nonprofit that provides such services in the El Paso, Texas, region and New Mexico. Lopez said her organization cannot afford its unaccompanied children’s legal program in west Texas.

“We are owed a significant amount of money — nearly a million dollars — for our program,” Lopez said. “We are not able to sustain this program without this contract.”

She said, come Friday afternoon, she would have to terminate the staff working on the program that they’d spent 20 years developing.

Lopez said the loss would be significant for the region, which she described as a “legal desert.”

“We are in an area where there aren’t enough attorneys for the community regardless of the type of case that they might have,” she said.

El Paso, she said, is also home to one of the largest detention centers in the U.S.

Meena Shah, managing director of legal services at the Door, a nonprofit in New York, says the federal government owes her organization about $2 million for legal services it has provided to unaccompanied children. She worries about losing access to her clients and other children, who will now be forced to face a complex immigration system alone.

“It’s preposterous to think that a child would be able to self-represent,” she said, “and I think any rational adult would agree with that.”

Problems began in March 2025, when the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services terminated its federal contract with the Washington-based Acacia Center for Justice. The nonprofit subcontracts with around 100 legal service providers nationwide who represent tens of thousands of unaccompanied children. The contract was up for renewal that same month.

That prompted the center and a coalition of nonprofit legal providers to file a federal class-action lawsuit against the agency and the Trump administration, alleging they were in violation of the William Wilberforce Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, a federal law enacted by Congress in 2008.

The law ensures unaccompanied children have legal counsel to represent them in legal proceedings and to protect them from mistreatment, exploitation and trafficking.

Since the law’s enactment, Congress has provided funding for the national program. In 2024, it set aside about $5 billion to fund the program through September 2027.

In June 2025, a federal judge in California ordered the Trump administration to reinstate the Acacia Center for Justice’s contract and continue to fund the program. Since then, the contract has been extended, but it is set to expire Friday.

Problems worsened in November when the Trump administration stopped paying its invoices as it demanded that the Acacia Center and its subcontractors provide information about clients that legal service providers say violates attorney-client privilege.

The coalition nonprofits say a federal court hearing has been scheduled for Aug. 6 to address the issues.

Legal service providers said at the heart of the matter is upholding due process, protecting children from exploitation and ensuring the federal government follows its own laws.

Michael Lukens, executive director of the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said the Trump administration’s refusal to reimburse nonprofits is an effort to prevent them from doing that.

“They are clearly trying to destroy the program by grinding down the financial health of nonprofits,” he said. “We’ve seen layoffs and furloughs, and we will see a lot more of that if these invoices aren’t paid.”

Last month, Kids in Need of Defense said in a written statement that it was canceling its subcontract with the Acacia Center for Justice after it had accrued more than $20 million in unpaid legal feels for assisting immigrant children.

But also in June, U.S. Rep. Zoe Lofgren (D-San José), a former immigration law professor, re-introduced the Fair Day in Court for Kids Act, a bill that would provide unaccompanied children with legal representation during proceedings in immigration courts.

“It’s absolutely heartbreaking and nonsensical to see children as young as 4 years old, unable to speak English, showing up to immigration court to face these complex proceedings alone,” she said in a statement at the time.

A number of current and former federal, state and local prosecutors sent a signed letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. raising law enforcement and humanitarian concerns about the program ending without a set plan.

Toczylowski said termination of a program that serves one of the most vulnerable immigrant populations should be viewed as an attack on children and Americans should be alarmed.

“When you take lawyers away from children, you do not just take away legal representation, you remove one of the few meaningful checks on government misconduct,” she said. “We have always said that our presence next to a child in a courtroom is one of the only things that gives them a fighting chance at justice in our broken immigration system.”

title: Scarborough calls on Congress to investigate activities at local ICE facility
description:
Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.
ICE in Maine Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center.
The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells.
The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC.
Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly protested outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.
text:
Members of the Scarborough Town Council voted Wednesday to pass a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to look into the operations of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement processing facility in the town after a federal agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford earlier this month.

But residents who spoke at the town council meeting said the proclamation doesn’t go far enough.

“We’re not in charge of federal immigration policy, but all eyes in Maine are on us as the only town that hosts a facility,” said Mary Ellen Galante, a Scarborough resident and retired nurse midwife, who objected to the proclamation because it “places all of the responsibility for action on our federal delegation and not on our town.”

Galante was among the roughly 70 people who attended the packed meeting, while more than 50 others braved the rain outside holding signs calling to get ICE out of Maine.

New restrictions on state involvement in immigration enforcement take effect Wednesday

The killing of 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero on July 13 has renewed scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement in Maine and many residents have called for local and state leaders to do more to protect communities in the state.

The question of how much power a community has to challenge federal activities within its jurisdiction is one that has wracked the state since President Donald Trump’s administration launched its enhanced enforcement operation in January. Several new laws took effect Wednesday that limit local cooperation with federal immigration agencies.

ICE in Maine

Unlike many other states, Maine does not have a standalone ICE detention center. The Scarborough processing facility is an administrative building for routine check-ins with three small, short-term holding cells. Detainees have historically been held in local jails or transferred to detention centers in Massachusetts or New Hampshire, or as far as Texas.

But during the meeting, several speakers raised concerns that ICE was misrepresenting what was occurring at that location.

“I think there are legitimate questions about whether the ordinances and the plans that have been put into place are consistent with what is happening in practice there,” Maine Rep. Sophie Warren, a Democrat who represents Scarborough, told Maine Morning Star. Warren presented a petition signed by more than 370 Mainers, 175 of which are Scarborough residents, calling on the council to take specific actions, including formally investigating the operations at the ICE facility and enforcing local laws and other municipal tools to rein in unlawful activities, which she said has precedence in Oregon.

The U.S. General Services Administration, which manages federal real estate, leased the facility from owner AEY, LLC. According to the agency’s lease inventory, the current 15-year lease began in 2021.

Since ICE arrived at the site, local community members have regularly protested outside the facility, and hundreds demonstrated in Scarborough the day after Guerrero was killed.

U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts made an unannounced visit to the facility on July 17, during which he said he confirmed that is where the officer who shot Guerrero works.

In December, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree also visited the building on Manson Libby Rd. after concerns were raised about attorneys not being permitted to accompany their clients to routine check-ins.

Josh Soley, the leasing and property manager for the building, said the GSA has the authority to subleaseto whichever agency they choose and that neither the state nor landlord has a say in who occupies the building.

Soley said he’s in support of the protests but believes the facility has nothing to do with what happened in Biddeford. He said people are “trying to find a place to put their voice, but I think it needs to be better targeted.”

But Scarborough councilmember Jon Anderson said that he believes Soley “must be part of this conversation.” Anderson said residents should know whether the company intends to extend the lease when it expires, and said Soley should also explore whether there’s a “mutually agreeable path” to end the lease arrangement with GSA early, “given the tragedy that occurred from the ICE agent employed at that facility.”

GSA declined to comment on the proclamation or the terms of the current lease agreement.

“I have a 20-page lease that I need to re-sign every single year and it asks me not to do unlawful activity,” Scarborough resident Sarah Lunt told the council. She added, “I would assume that that includes murdering someone in cold blood.”

Proclamation details

The proclamation asks Maine’s congressional delegation to engage with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and other agencies to review the facility and evaluate alternatives, “including the relocation or discontinuation of such operations at that location.”

It further asks for transparency and community engagement regarding federal immigration enforcement activities and for the delegation to “ensure that federal actions conducted within Maine respect human dignity, civil rights, public trust, due process, and community safety and commit to raising concerns with federal officials should evidence emerge that these standards are not being upheld.”

The town notes the proclamation should not be interpreted as opposition to lawful immigration enforcement but rather, the “expectation that such enforcement be conducted in a manner consistent with the values of safety, transparency, accountability, and respect for all people.”

While a handful of residents expressed concern that the resolution was beyond the purview of the council and would open the town to lawsuits from the federal government, the vast majority who spoke said they supported the proclamation as a first step for the town to take.

Congressional support

Ahead of the meeting, Pingree, who represents the southern Maine district that includes Biddeford and Scarborough, told the Scarborough council that the town “has every right to ask whether continuing to host this facility serves the interests of the community.”

“In my view, that question deserves serious consideration from the Department of Homeland Security,” Pingree wrote in a letter. “When a federal facility reaches the point where its very presence undermines the public confidence and leaves residents feeling less safe, the federal government has a responsibility to reconsider if that facility belongs there at all.”

Pingree added that she’s “exploring every available avenue to address enforcement operations and the continued presence of ICE in Scarborough.”

U.S. Sens. Angus King and Susan Collins, and U.S. Rep. Jared Golden did not comment on the proclamation. They previously sent a joint letter to the DHS Inspector General calling for a full, transparent investigation into the shooting and King has called for a review of ICE protocol.
